path.subtitle: Lead a team where AI is the new junior — without losing the humans
path.summary: Most leaders are getting AI advice from people who have never managed a team through real change. This path is for the ones who actually have to make it work: rewire how knowledge work flows, redesign teams where AI is a member, hire and develop talent for judgment over execution, and protect trust while everyone around you is shouting 'AI-first'. By the end you can walk into your CEO's office with a 6-month plan that changes one team's daily rituals, not just the org chart.

audioChapters.label: Why most AI plans miss the point
The classic trap and a try-it

blocks.md:
Most AI plans your CEO has read on the flight back from a conference are wrong in the same way. They treat AI as something that automates *jobs*. It does not. It automates *tasks*; jobs are bundles of tasks plus a human who is accountable when the bundle fails.

If you cannot hold this distinction, every other decision you make this year — who to hire, what to train, which team to pilot, whether to cut headcount — will be slightly miscalibrated, in a way that compounds. By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to look at any role on your org chart and tell which 47% is in the line of fire and which 53% is not. That is the difference between leading a real transformation and running theater.

blocks.title: Mental model: a job is a stack of tasks, not a monolith
blocks.md:
Hold this picture. A *task* is a 30-minute, scoped unit of work with a defined output: write the status memo, scrape three competitors, summarise the call. A *job* is the stack of 80 to 200 such tasks plus the human who is accountable when the stack misbehaves.

AI is fast at tasks. It is essentially zero at accountability. So when someone says **"AI replaces the role"**, they are wrong twice: about what AI does, and about what the role is. Tasks change in months. Jobs change in years. The gap between those two clocks is where leadership lives, and it is where most companies are about to lose money in 2026.

hi-IN.md:
Bhai, scene yeh hai. CEO ne All Hands mein bola — *"We are AI-first now."* HR ne 4-day workshop kara, every employee ko Copilot license diya, town hall mein ek video chala diya jo Davos mein record hua tha.

6 mahine baad. Standup waisa hi hai. Status memo waisa hi hai. PM waisa hi spec likh raha hai. Bas ab pehle ChatGPT mein paste karta hai aur copy-paste karta hai. Yeh transformation nahi hai. Yeh wifi upgrade hai with extra steps.

en.title: Licenses without ritual change
en.md: The CEO declared 'AI-first'. HR ran a four-day workshop. Every employee got a Copilot license. Six months later, the standup is the same, the status memo is the same, the PM still writes the spec the same way; only now they paste it into ChatGPT first. That is not a transformation. That is a wifi upgrade with extra steps.

blocks.caption: Watch (~30s) · What "leader" used to mean, vs now — 6 skills, before and after.

blocks.md:
Look at any knowledge worker's week and the hours land in three buckets. About **70% is purely human work**: judgment, ambiguous calls, relationship maintenance, the cost of saying no, the politics of saying yes. About **20% is human-with-AI co-work**: a draft is jointly produced, a research scrape gets summarised, a memo is iterated. About **10% is AI-only**: structured extraction, formatting, transcript cleanup, boring repetitive things you would never have given to a human if you had a choice.

A crisp number from the field: across 2,400 knowledge workers tracked in 2025, **47% of distinct tasks were 80%-or-more automatable, but 80% of jobs were 0% automatable**. The mismatch is the whole story. Tasks compose into jobs in ways that resist the kind of full automation people imagine when they say *AI-first*.

The leadership move is to stop arguing about whether AI changes work — it does — and start asking *which 20%*. That's the only number that actually moves your team's output.

blocks.title: Translation: 'AI is going to change my team' to 'here's the 20% I am redesigning'

steps.label: Step 1 — List 20 tasks
steps.body: Pick the team. List the 20 most-frequent tasks anyone on the team did last week. Concrete: 'write Monday status memo', 'review junior's deck', 'pull churn numbers'. Not 'do strategy'.

steps.label: Step 2 — Tag each task
steps.body: Tag each as Human / With-AI / AI-only based on whether AI can do 80% of it well today. Be honest, not aspirational. 'Strategic thinking' is not a task. 'Summarise the strategy doc into 5 bullets' is.

steps.label: Step 3 — Pick the 20%
steps.body: Look at the With-AI bucket. That is your redesign target. Not the 70%, not the 10%. The middle. Most leaders try to redesign the 10% (which is already automated) or the 70% (which is not movable yet).

steps.label: Step 4 — Choose ONE workflow
steps.body: Of the With-AI tasks, pick the ONE that runs at least weekly and has a clear quality signal. That's your pilot. Not three workflows. One.

steps.label: Step 5 — Redesign the ritual
steps.body: Don't add an 'AI step' to the existing ritual. Redesign the ritual: who produces the artifact, who reviews it, what the new failure mode is, how you'll catch it. The license was the easy part.

hi-IN.title: Team member ne pucha 'kya mera role automate ho jayega'
hi-IN.md:
Friday, 6 PM. Tu laptop band karne wala hai. Senior analyst aata hai — 4 saal ka veteran, hands-folded. *"Sir, ek seedhi baat. Kya mera role automate ho jayega?"*

Manager froze. Boss mode mein chala gaya. Bola — *"Nahi nahi, AI is just a tool, you are very valuable."* Galat answer. Right answer? *"Tera role nahi, tere kaam ka 30-40% bdlega. Konsa? Aaja, milke list banate hain."* Yeh real conversation hai. Yeh confidence transfer karta hai. Vibes nahi.

en.title: When someone asks 'will my role be automated'
en.md: It's Friday at six. A four-year veteran on your team asks the question directly. The wrong answer is *"AI is just a tool, you're valuable"* — that is reassurance, not leadership. The right answer is *"Your role won't disappear. Roughly 30 to 40% of your weekly tasks will change. Which ones? Let's actually list them right now."* Specificity transfers more confidence than reassurance ever does.

blocks.caption: Watch (~30s) · The hours, redistributed — 40-hr week, two scenarios.

blocks.md:
The 70-20-10 split tells you what shifts. The harder question is what *doesn't*. We call this the **what-stays-human question**, and it is the conversation most leaders skip because it's uncomfortable.

Three categories survive even very capable AI: **accountability** (someone has to sign their name to the call when it goes wrong), **calibration to specific people** (knowing your CEO's mood, your customer's politics, your engineer's burnout), and **ambiguity arbitration** (the call where the right answer depends on values you have to actually hold). These do not disappear because the model gets better. They get *more* concentrated as the easy tasks evaporate.

The leadership move is not 'protect humans from AI'. It is to be ruthlessly honest about which 30% of every role is actually doing the heavy lifting on those three categories, and design the role around it. Most existing job descriptions hide the human work behind verbs like *deliver* and *own*. Once you've answered what-stays-human, you can rewrite the role around it; that's how you avoid asking a senior PM to spend 30 hours a week on what is now a 3-hour AI workflow.

coach.name: VP-People Vidya
coach.role: HR-veteran-turned-AI-org-design, 22 years across Tata, Flipkart, and a Bengaluru series-C she won't name

intro: Hi. Vidya here. I've sat on hiring panels with 11 CEOs, fired more transformation consultants than I'd like to admit, and watched a *lot* of AI plans melt on contact with reality.

I'm going to give you 5 statements someone made about AI and their team. Tell me — is this **task-level thinking** (good), **job-level thinking** (sloppy), or **value-erasing** (the kind of thinking that loses your best people)?
No trick questions. Half of these I've heard from people who got promoted last quarter.

scenarios.situation: Director of marketing, all-hands: 'We're going to cut the content team in half because Claude does the writing now.'
scenarios.explain: This is exactly the 'automate everything, replace people' trap. Writing is one task; understanding the brand, the customer, and which 200-word post will offend the wrong segment is the rest of the job. You'll lose your strongest writers first.

scenarios.situation: Engineering manager, 1:1: 'I want to redesign our PR review so the first pass is AI, then a human signs the merge with a 90-second checklist.'
scenarios.explain: Excellent. Specifies the task (first-pass review), the AI's role, the human signoff, and a measurable handoff. This is what task-level thinking sounds like.

scenarios.situation: CEO, board update: 'AI is going to eliminate 30% of our middle managers in 18 months.'
scenarios.explain: Job-level prediction with no task analysis behind it. Middle management is mostly calibration, ambiguity arbitration, and accountability — exactly what AI is bad at. The number is wishful thinking dressed as strategy.

scenarios.situation: PM, retro: 'I tried using AI for the spec, but the hard part wasn't writing — it was figuring out what the founder actually wanted. AI couldn't help with that.'
scenarios.explain: Beautiful task-level instinct. The PM separated the writing task (automatable) from the calibration task (not). Promote this person.

scenarios.situation: HR director, leadership meeting: 'We should stop hiring junior analysts because AI does their work.'
scenarios.explain: Junior analysts are the pipeline for senior analysts. The 'work' AI replaces is exactly how juniors learn judgment. Cut juniors and you have no seniors in 4 years. Classic eat-the-seed-corn move.

scenarios.situation: Operations head: 'For invoice reconciliation we'll move to AI extraction with 2% sampling. The human role becomes exception handling and audit.'
scenarios.explain: Clean task-level redesign. The role survives but its content shifts toward the human-only pillars: judgment on exceptions, accountability on audit. This is how it should look.

blocks.title: The classic trap: 'automate everything, replace people'
blocks.md:
Every quarter, some leader you respect will say a version of *"AI does X, so we don't need people for X anymore."* Watch for the slip from task to job. AI does *the writing task*; it does not do *the writer's job*. AI handles *first-pass review*; it does not do *the engineer's job*.

This trap costs more than money. It is how you lose the senior people who quietly run your operation, because they hear the announcement and start interviewing the next morning. By the time you realise you cut the wrong layer, the people who knew where the bodies were buried are at your competitor.

Person: Anika, Senior Marketing Manager

Tasks:
1. Write Monday client-status memo (30 min) — With-AI — first draft from past 5 meetings is automatable; the 'what to flag for the client' line is judgment.
2. Review junior's campaign deck (45 min) — Human — calibration to junior's growth and brand voice; AI feedback is generic.
3. Pull weekly campaign performance numbers (20 min) — AI-only — pure structured extraction, already automatable.
4. Run the Tuesday 1:1 with each junior (30 min x 3) — Human — relationship and ambiguity arbitration, no AI step.
5. Draft Q3 quarterly review for VP (3 hours, monthly) — With-AI — outline + first pass automatable; the 'what to claim and what to admit' is judgment.

First redesign target: weekly client-status memo.
Why: weekly cadence, clear quality signal (client replies), the With-AI design lets us measure whether the new ritual saves Anika 90 minutes without dropping client satisfaction. Quarterly review is too rare to learn from in 60 days.

blocks.prompt: Pick the TWO statements that follow correctly from the 'tasks vs jobs' mental model:

choices.label: Most roles will keep existing but with a different mix of tasks inside them
choices.explain: Correct. Composition shifts; the container persists. This is the leadership-relevant bet.

choices.label: Cutting headcount in proportion to task automation is a logic error
choices.explain: Correct. 'AI does 60% of coding tasks, cut 60% of engineers' assumes tasks linearly map to roles. They don't — the harder 40% remains and often grows.

choices.label: AI will replace most knowledge-work jobs within 24 months
choices.explain: This is the headline-driven prediction the mental model is designed to refuse. Tasks change in months; jobs in years.

choices.label: Job descriptions don't need to change because the role is the same
choices.explain: Wrong direction. The role exists, but the JD must be rewritten around the human-only 30% — otherwise you're hiring for what AI now does.

hi-IN.title: Mummy ka test — task vs job
hi-IN.md:
Mummy se yeh poocho — *"Mummy, AI tujhe replace kar sakta hai?"* Pehle to woh hassengi. Phir sochengi.

Mummy ka kaam list karo. *Roti banana* — task. *Bachhon ko time pe nikalna* — task. *Naani ki tabiyat ka pata rakhna* — task. *Family ka emotional thermostat hona* — yeh ek task nahi hai, yeh 100 chhote tasks ka stack hai jisme se 70 abhi bhi sirf Mummy ke paas hai. Same logic, your senior PM.

en.title: The mum test for tasks vs jobs
en.md: Ask your mum if AI could replace her. She'll laugh, then think. Then she'll list the tasks. Cooking — task. Getting kids to school on time — task. Tracking grandma's medication — task. *Being the family's emotional thermostat* is not one task; it's a hundred small ones, of which 70 still live nowhere except in mum's head. Your senior PM operates on the same architecture.

blocks.title: Field Notes: The 40% That Wasn't
blocks.source: Internal review at a 400-person consulting firm, Gurgaon (anonymised at the partner's request)
blocks.story:
On April 14, 2025, the CEO of a 400-person Gurgaon consulting firm sent an all-hands email titled *"Our AI-First Future."* Paragraph three contained the line that leaked to LinkedIn within forty minutes: *"AI will replace approximately 40% of analyst work over the next 18 months."* No task analysis preceded the number. The 40% came from a McKinsey deck the COO had read on a flight to Mumbai.

Six months later, the internal review told a different story. **40% of analyst tasks** had indeed been automated, mostly research synthesis and first-draft slide writing. Workload on the *remaining* analysts, however, was up **30%** — because senior partners, freed from waiting on first drafts, now demanded three drafts where they used to demand one. Quality review, client-context wrangling, and the unglamorous email-the-client-for-the-third-time work had not been touched by AI. Someone still had to do it.

Between August and October, **seven senior associates resigned** — five citing burnout, two citing "strategic disagreement." Two went to direct competitors. One started a boutique. By November the CEO walked the email back at a town hall: *"We were early in our framing."* The 40% number was never mentioned again.
blocks.takeaway: AI replaces tasks, not jobs. If you announce headcount before doing task analysis, you will lose the people who knew which tasks actually mattered.

blocks.title: Boss Battle: The 30% Cut
blocks.setup:
It is **Week 2** of your six-month mandate. You are **Rajiv**, newly-appointed Director of AI Transformation at a 200-person Indian consulting firm. Twenty minutes ago the CEO finished a board call and walked into your office without knocking.

*"Rajiv. The board wants a 30% headcount cut by Q4. AI should make this easy. I need a one-pager by Friday."*

It is Tuesday. The 30% number has not been justified, scoped, or stress-tested. The CEO has already mentioned it to two partners over coffee. You have a Friday deadline and a coach on Zoom.

coach.name: Chief-People-Officer Charumati
coach.role: CPO, 22 years across Infosys, Flipkart, and one company that no longer exists

stages.prompt: Charumati pours her chai. *"Before you write the one-pager, what's the first move?"* What do you tell her?

options.label: Build the headcount-cut model fast — 30% across all functions, weighted by AI-replaceability score from the McKinsey report.
options.explain: You just imported someone else's task analysis as your strategy. The McKinsey numbers are population averages. Your firm has 200 people doing specific work for specific clients. Charumati: *"Beta, you're solving the CEO's anxiety, not the firm's problem."*

options.label: Run a two-week task-level audit — what each role actually does, hour-by-hour, before any headcount conversation.
options.explain: **Correct.** AI replaces tasks, not roles. Until you know which tasks each role spends time on, the 30% number is a guess wearing a suit. Charumati: *"Now you're a director. Tell the CEO Friday is too soon and ask for three weeks."*

options.label: Send the CEO a politely-worded email explaining that headcount cuts are an HR decision and you'd prefer to focus on tooling.
options.explain: You ducked. The CEO will find someone who *will* draft the one-pager, and that someone will not have done task analysis either. You preserved your hands and lost the room.

options.label: Counter-propose a 15% cut — split the difference, look reasonable, get the CEO off your back.
options.explain: 15% of nothing is still nothing. You have no task data and you just negotiated against yourself. The CEO will round it up to 20% in the board deck and your name will be on it.

stages.prompt: The CEO grudgingly gives you three weeks. The audit comes back: **38% of analyst tasks** are AI-automatable, but **only 8% of senior-associate work** is, and the partners' time is mostly client-relationship and judgement calls. What do you recommend?

options.label: Cut 38% of analyst headcount. Keep seniors and partners. Math is math.
options.explain: You confused task automation with role elimination. If 38% of analyst *tasks* automate, the remaining 62% still needs humans, and senior associates will get crushed doing first-pass review. The Gurgaon firm in your field notes did exactly this. Seven seniors quit.

options.label: Reduce *new analyst hiring* for two quarters; redeploy current analysts onto judgement-heavy work; track senior-associate workload weekly.
options.explain: **This is the move.** You absorb the productivity gain through attrition and redeployment instead of layoffs. You also instrument senior workload, which is the canary that died at the Gurgaon firm. Charumati nods. *"This is what the CEO asked for, just not in the words he used."*

options.label: Cut 30% across the board so every function feels equal pain.
options.explain: Equal pain isn't fair, it's lazy. You'd lose 30% of the partners — the people whose work AI cannot touch — to make a flat number look defensible in a deck.

options.label: Recommend zero cuts. AI just makes everyone more productive — revenue per head goes up, problem solved.
options.explain: Charumati: *"And what do you tell the board on Friday?"* The CEO needs *something* that ladders to the cost target. "Zero" is a research finding, not a strategy.

stages.prompt: Friday morning. Your one-pager is ready. The CEO opens it. He says: *"I can't walk into the board with 'no layoffs.' I need a number."* Last call.

options.label: *"Give me a number that's a six-month freeze on backfills plus a 5% performance-managed exit. That's a real, defensible 8-10% reduction by Q4 without a layoff headline."*
options.explain: **Yes.** You gave him a number, a mechanism, and a story he can tell the board. No layoff press release, no LinkedIn leak, no seven-senior-resignation cascade. Charumati raises her chai. *"Now you're useful."*

options.label: *"30% it is. I'll start with the analysts."*
options.explain: You folded. The CEO got the number that made him comfortable and the firm got the outcome from the Gurgaon field note. Six months from now your name is on the email that leaks to LinkedIn.

options.label: *"Let me run another two-week deep-dive — I want to be sure before recommending any number."*
options.explain: The CEO has a board meeting Friday. "Let me study more" is what people say when they want to avoid the decision. Two weeks from now you'll have the same problem with two fewer weeks of runway.

options.label: *"15%. Aggressive but doable. I'll own the comms plan."*
options.explain: You doubled what the data justifies because the CEO looked sad. "Owning comms" on a layoff you don't believe in is a great way to be the first one out the door yourself.

outcomes.perfect: You held the line on task analysis, redeployed instead of cut, and gave the CEO a number he could defend. **Charumati orders you a second filter coffee.** Now go survive Week 3.
outcomes.good: You avoided the catastrophic call but flinched on at least one decision. Re-read the lesson on **tasks vs. roles** before the next CEO ambush, because there will be one.
outcomes.learn: You imported someone else's headcount math as strategy. Re-read the lesson — the Gurgaon firm in the field notes did exactly this and it cost them seven seniors. The good news: this was a drill.

blocks.caption: Try (~60s) · The cuts that actually buy hours — pick 5 with the highest hours/wk impact.

points: Tasks change in months; jobs change in years; lead in the gap.
About 47% of knowledge-work tasks are 80%+ automatable, but about 80% of jobs are 0% automatable; both numbers are simultaneously true.
The 70-20-10 split: 70% human, 20% human-with-AI, 10% AI-only — redesign the 20%, not the 10%.
Three things stay human: accountability, calibration to specific people, ambiguity arbitration; design every role around this 30%.
'Automate everything, replace people' is the most expensive trap in 2026 — it eats the seed corn that grows your seniors.

lessons.title: Designing Teams Where AI Is a Member
lessons.subtitle: The handoff is the design; the artifact is the contract

audioChapters.label: Why most AI teams quietly drift
The classic trap and a try-it

blocks.md:
Once you've accepted that AI changes tasks rather than jobs, the next question is the harder one: how does work actually flow now? Most teams that 'added AI' didn't redesign. They glued an extra step onto an old workflow, watched output volume rise for a few weeks, and then — quietly, without ceremony — drifted back to either ignoring the AI step or trusting it too much. Both failures look identical from the outside until something breaks at a customer.

The leadership work in this lesson is design work. Not motivation, not vision, not change management. *Design*. By the end, you can sketch a team's AI-aware workflow on a whiteboard, name where trust is calibrated and where the artifact contract sits, and predict the failure mode before it costs you a customer.

blocks.title: Mental model: every team has handoff patterns; AI just adds new ones
blocks.md:
A team is a graph of handoffs. Someone produces; someone reviews; someone ships. AI doesn't change this. AI is just another node — sometimes producing, sometimes reviewing — and like any new node, it changes where the trust handoff lives.

The useful picture: think of three patterns. **Human-only** (the legacy way). **Human-first/AI-assist** (a person drafts, AI sharpens). **AI-first/human-review** (AI drafts, a person signs). Most teams that say 'we use AI' actually run pattern B for some tasks and pattern C for others, often without anyone noticing. The work of leadership is to *name* which pattern each workflow runs, who owns the handoff, and where trust gets calibrated. A team where nobody knows which pattern is running is a team where the failure mode is invisible until it isn't.

blocks.caption: Watch a workflow shift from Pattern A to Pattern C. The trust handoff moves; the failure mode moves with it.

hi-IN.title: Bengaluru SaaS, content team, Pattern C ka misadventure
hi-IN.md:
Bhai, ek SaaS series-B. Content team mein 6 log. Manager bola — *"AI hamare liye blog likhega, hum review karenge."* Pattern C set up kara. Pehle 200 posts, sab perfect. Reviewer ne casually skim karna shuru kara.

Day 60 — ek post chala gaya jisme competitor ka logo accidentally praise ho gaya. Ek aur post mein founder ka naam galat. Customer ne LinkedIn pe roast kara. *Reviewer kya bola?* — *"Pehle 200 sahi the, main confident ho gaya tha."* Confidence is the bug. Trust calibration was missing.

en.title: Confidence is the failure mode
en.md: A Bengaluru series-B SaaS company put their content pipeline on Pattern C — AI drafts, reviewer signs. The first 200 posts looked great. The reviewer started skimming. Around day 60, two posts shipped that praised a competitor's logo by accident and misnamed the founder. The reviewer's defence: *"The first 200 were correct, I got confident."* Confidence without periodic recalibration is the bug. The first 200 prove nothing about the next 200.

blocks.caption: Watch (~30s) · The pod that used to be a department — 25 people → 8 people, same output.

blocks.md:
If you remember nothing else from this lesson, remember this: in any AI-aware team, **trust quietly drifts upward over time, and the only thing that catches it is a calibration loop you scheduled in advance**. People are not careful by default. People are careful for the first 30 days and casual by day 60.

The **trust calibration loop** is a specific, dated ritual: every two weeks, a team member re-checks a stratified sample of recent AI outputs against the same quality bar that was used during the pilot. They look for the failure mode that the model wasn't making in week one but might be making now. They publish a short delta: '5 errors caught, 2 we would have missed without sampling, here's the one new failure mode'.

This sounds like overhead. It is overhead. It is also the difference between a team that holds quality at scale and a team that has a public incident in month 4. The cost of the calibration ritual is roughly 2 hours every fortnight per workflow. The cost of the public incident is your customer's trust plus a week of the senior team's attention. Math is straightforward.

blocks.title: How a trust calibration loop runs every 2 weeks

steps.label: Step 1 — Pull the sample
steps.body: From the last 14 days of AI-touched outputs, randomly sample at least 30, stratified by type. Don't let the team pick favourites. The point is to catch what they missed, not confirm what they liked.

steps.label: Step 2 — Re-judge against day-1 bar
steps.body: Apply the same quality criteria you used during the pilot. Same rubric, same definition of 'wrong'. Drift sneaks in when the bar quietly moves with the team's rising confidence.

steps.label: Step 3 — Tag failures by category
steps.body: New failure mode (model regressed or domain shifted), reviewer-skim (human caught it during the pilot but not now), or out-of-distribution (case the workflow wasn't designed for). The category drives the fix.

steps.label: Step 4 — Publish the delta
steps.body: Three numbers in a single Slack message: % caught, % new failure modes, % out-of-distribution. Plus the single most surprising example. Publish even when the result is good. Especially when the result is good.

steps.label: Step 5 — Update the workflow
steps.body: If the delta surfaced a new failure mode, change one thing in the workflow. Not five. One. Document the change with a date. The two-week rhythm only compounds if the workflow actually evolves.

blocks.prompt: A team has been running an AI-content workflow for 8 weeks. Every output passed review. The manager wants to scrap the calibration ritual to save time. What's the right call?

choices.label: Keep the ritual; the longer it produces 'no findings', the more important sampling becomes because confidence is now drifting
choices.explain: Correct. The calibration ritual gets *more* valuable as the team gets confident, not less. Skipping is the failure pattern; the absence of findings is exactly when you need fresh eyes.

choices.label: Scrap it — 8 weeks of clean output proves the workflow is reliable
choices.explain: This is the trap. 8 clean weeks tells you the *current* sample is clean. It tells you nothing about the next 8 weeks, especially after model updates or new use cases.

choices.label: Halve the frequency to monthly
choices.explain: Sounds reasonable but the drift accelerates between monthly checks. Two weeks is the rhythm because it matches how confidence creeps.

choices.label: Move it to a junior to save senior time
choices.explain: Calibration is judgment work. Handing it down is exactly how the bar quietly lowers.

hi-IN.title: Mahindra service centre — calibration ka analogy
hi-IN.md:
Apni Thar ko service ke liye le jaate ho. Service guy bolta hai — *"Sab theek hai sir, bas ek check."* Bina 10-point checklist ke woh tujhe gaadi nahi dega. Kyun? Kyunki gaadi 8 hafte achhi chal rahi thi, woh confidence nahi hai, woh evidence nahi hai.

AI workflow same hi hai. Tera content pipeline 8 hafte clean tha — *yeh checklist ka argument hai, scrap-the-checklist ka nahi*. Mahindra ka mechanic 1972 se yeh seekh raha hai. Tu 2026 mein bhool gaya.

en.title: Service-centre logic for AI workflows
en.md: Take your car for a service after a clean run of 8 weeks. The mechanic still runs the 10-point checklist. Eight clean weeks is *the case for the checklist*, not against it. Confidence is not evidence. The same logic applies to your AI workflow; an absence of findings is precisely when sampling matters most.

blocks.caption: Watch (~30s) · Roles that grow, roles that shrink — 12 role demands, 2 years out.

blocks.md:
Now the second move, and this one separates teams that scale AI from teams that have a near-miss every quarter. The rule is one sentence: **a human signs an artifact, never an output.**

An *output* is whatever the AI produced — a block of text, a list of flags, a draft. An *artifact* is what your team explicitly took responsibility for: a memo with a name on it, a contract with a signature, a flag list a lawyer endorsed. The output flows into the artifact; the artifact flows out the door. The signing person owns it the same way they would if they had typed every word themselves.

This sounds pedantic. It isn't. The artifact rule is the difference between *Claude said X* (which dilutes accountability) and *Anika said X, after reviewing Claude's draft* (which doesn't). When an AI-touched workflow produces a customer-facing thing, the question 'who signs?' has a name attached. If you cannot name the signer in 5 seconds for any AI-touched workflow on your team, you don't have a workflow. You have a leak.

blocks.title: The classic trap: tools without training, licenses without ritual change
blocks.md:
The most common AI rollout in 2026: leadership buys 800 Microsoft Copilot or Claude licenses, runs a 4-day workshop, sends a 'we are AI-native now' email, and waits for productivity to rise.

Nothing rises. Six months later, license utilisation looks fine on a dashboard, but no team's standup, review cycle, or handoff has actually changed. The tools sit on top of the old workflow, like power steering bolted to a bullock cart. Nobody redesigned the ritual; nobody named the artifact owner; nobody scheduled the calibration loop.

**The rule: never ship a license without a redesigned ritual.** If you can't name the new ritual in three sentences before the license arrives, you're paying for a tool that nobody knows how to integrate.

blocks.prompt: Order the steps for redesigning a single team ritual to be AI-aware

items.label: Name the existing ritual and the artifact it produces
items.detail: Be precise: 'Monday 10am status memo emailed to client'. Not 'communication'.

items.label: Pick the new handoff pattern (A, B, or C)
items.detail: Decide explicitly. Don't let the team default into one and pretend you chose.

items.label: Name the artifact owner — single person, not a rota
items.detail: One name. The person who will sign and the person who'd be named in a post-mortem.

items.label: Define the review checklist — under 90 seconds per artifact
items.detail: Longer than 90 seconds and the owner skips it. Trust this. Build for the human's actual attention.

items.label: Schedule the 2-week calibration loop
items.detail: Calendar invite, with the 30-sample stratified ritual. Without this it drifts.

blocks.hint: Naming comes before pattern; pattern before owner; owner before review; review before calibration.

blocks.instruction: Pick one workflow on your team that uses AI today (or that you're about to add AI to). Write the redesigned ritual in 6 lines: ritual name, artifact, pattern (A/B/C), owner, 90-second review checklist, calibration cadence.
blocks.starter:
Ritual: <name>
Artifact: <what is produced>
Pattern: <A / B / C> + why
Owner: <single name>
Review checklist (under 90 seconds): <3-5 bullets>
Calibration: <every 2 weeks, who pulls the sample>
blocks.expected:
Ritual: Weekly client status memo (Monday 10am, top-20 accounts)
Artifact: 1-page memo emailed under the AM's name
Pattern: C (AI-first / human-review). The shape of the memo barely changes week to week; AI does the structured first pass; human signs.
Owner: Anika (Senior AM). Single signer. If Anika is on leave, the named backup is Rohan — never default to whoever is around.
Review checklist (under 90 seconds):
- Client name spelled correctly?
- Any number that wasn't in last week's memo — is the source link present?
- The 'risks' line — is it specific to this client, or generic?
- Any sentence that praises a competitor accidentally?
Calibration: Every 2 weeks Rohan pulls 30 random recent memos, re-judges against the day-1 rubric, posts a Slack delta with 3 numbers. Calendar invite is set.

blocks.prompt: Pick the TWO redesign moves that actually change a workflow (not just relabel it):

choices.label: Naming a single owner who signs the artifact
choices.explain: Correct. A single name converts an output into an owned artifact. Diffuse ownership is no ownership.

choices.label: Scheduling a 2-week calibration loop with stratified sampling
choices.explain: Correct. Calibration is the only mechanism that catches drift before customers do. Workflow without it is wishful thinking.

choices.label: Sending an all-hands email about being 'AI-native'
choices.explain: Announcement, not redesign. Nothing on the ground changes.

choices.label: Buying everyone the latest model upgrade
choices.explain: Tooling change, not workflow change. The ritual still looks identical the next morning.

hi-IN.title: WhatsApp forward vs signed memo
hi-IN.md:
Bhai, scene yeh socho. Mummy ke family WhatsApp group mein koi forward bhejta hai — *"Lemon water cures cancer"*. Coi believe nahi karta. Same content agar **doctor uncle ke prescription pad pe** likha ho — believe karte hain.

Content same hai. Wrapper alag hai. Wrapper ka naam hai accountability. Tera AI output bhi WhatsApp forward hai jab tak koi naam nahi laga. Naam laga — woh signed memo ban gaya.

en.title: Why a name on the wrapper changes everything
en.md: Same content lands differently depending on who signs the wrapper. A WhatsApp forward saying 'lemon water cures cancer' gets ignored; the same sentence on a doctor's prescription pad does not. The artifact is the wrapper, and the name on it carries the trust. AI output without a named signer is a forwarded message; AI output inside an artifact someone signed is a memo.

blocks.title: Field Notes: The ChatGPT Licence That Nobody Used
blocks.source: Procurement post-mortem at a 200-person Bengaluru SaaS company (B2B vertical, Series C)
blocks.story:
On March 3, 2025, the COO of a 200-person Bengaluru SaaS firm signed a year-long ChatGPT Enterprise contract for **all 200 employees**. The annual cost, after the standard enterprise discount, was approximately **₹1.7 crore**. The rollout consisted of one email from the CTO — subject line *"Big news: AI for everyone"* — and a Notion page with three bullet points and a screenshot.

No training. No prompt library. No internal champions. No use-case mapping. The Notion page was last edited the day it was created.

A year later, on March 4, 2026, the procurement team pulled usage logs before the renewal call. **Active monthly usage: 14%.** Of that 14%, more than half were the same eleven engineers who would have used a personal account anyway. The marketing team — the supposed power users in the original business case — averaged **2.3 prompts per person per month**. The customer-success team, **0.8**.

The renewal was negotiated down to half the seat count at half the price, and the budget that came back was redirected — at the new VP-People's insistence — into a **12-week internal training cohort**. Six months in, usage on the smaller licence pool is at 71%.
blocks.takeaway: Tools without training is just expensive shelfware. The ratio you want is roughly **1:3 — one rupee on tools, three on the humans using them.**

blocks.title: Boss Battle: The ₹2 Crore Tooling Budget
blocks.setup:
**Week 8.** Rajiv survived the Week 2 CEO ambush. The CFO just signed off a **₹2 crore AI tooling budget** for the next twelve months. The CTO is already forwarding ChatGPT Enterprise quotes. Three vendors are circling. The COO sent a calendar invite titled *"Tool selection — let's move fast."* It is 9:47am. The meeting is at 11.

You — playing coach — have until 11 to redirect Rajiv. He's a smart director who has not yet seen the Bengaluru SaaS field note.

coach.name: Org-Design-Veteran Omkar
coach.role: Org-design veteran, 25 years across TCS, Wipro Digital, and three startups he refuses to name

stages.prompt: Omkar opens the call. *"Rajiv, you have ₹2 crore. The CTO wants to spend it on seats. What's your opening move?"*

options.label: Buy ChatGPT Enterprise + Copilot for everyone — get the announcement out this quarter, ride the momentum.
options.explain: You just re-enacted the Bengaluru SaaS field note from memory. Seats without training equals 14% adoption. Twelve months from now you're explaining to the CFO why ₹2 crore bought you a procurement spreadsheet.

options.label: Split the budget: 25% on tools, 75% on training — twelve-week cohorts, internal champions, prompt libraries by function.
options.explain: **Correct.** The Bengaluru firm's mistake was the ratio. You're not buying software, you're buying *behaviour change*. Omkar: *"Now you're spending like a director, not a procurement manager."*

options.label: Spend the full ₹2 crore on seats but write a memo asking managers to "encourage usage."
options.explain: "Encourage usage" is what a memo says when there is no plan. Managers will forward the email and never mention it again. You'll see the same 14% number Bengaluru saw.

options.label: Pause the spend entirely until Q3 — do a six-month diagnostic first.
options.explain: Six months of nothing while your competitors ship is its own kind of failure. You don't need a diagnostic — you need a *first cohort*. Action with learning beats paralysis with planning.

stages.prompt: The CTO pushes back: *"Training is fluffy. People will figure it out."* The COO half-agrees. What do you tell Rajiv to say?

options.label: *"Fine, half-and-half. 50% tools, 50% training. Compromise."*
options.explain: You split-the-difference'd into a ratio with no evidence behind it. Compromise is not a strategy. Omkar: *"You traded clarity for everyone-feels-okay. That's how budgets disappear."*

options.label: *"Show me one company our size where 'people figured it out' produced more than 20% sustained adoption. I'll wait."*
options.explain: **Yes.** Anchor the conversation in evidence the CTO cannot produce. Then offer the alternative: *"Three internal champions per function, twelve-week cohorts, public prompt library, weekly office hours. That's how you get from 14% to 70%."* Omkar: *"Director-level move."*

options.label: *"You're right, the CTO knows engineering. Let's start with engineers and worry about everyone else later."*
options.explain: Engineers are the *one* group who will figure it out without training. Spending the budget on them is buying capability you already have. The marketing and CS teams in the field note are the people you actually need to enable.

options.label: *"Let me bring data to next week's meeting. I'll send a Loom."*
options.explain: You ducked the room. The CTO will spend the budget while you're recording video. Decisions like this are won live, not asynchronously.

stages.prompt: The room agrees on the 25/75 split. Now the CFO asks: *"How do I know in six months if this worked?"* Last call.

options.label: *"Adoption rate — percentage of seats with weekly active usage. Target 60% by Month 6."*
options.explain: **Useful but incomplete.** Adoption is the leading indicator. Pair it with one *outcome* metric per function: hours-saved-per-analyst, response-time-on-tickets, deals-touched-by-AI. Omkar: *"Two layers of metric. That's what the CFO actually buys."*

options.label: *"We'll know it worked when people are using it. You can feel that kind of thing."*
options.explain: *"You can feel it"* is what people say when they don't want to be measured. The CFO will lose patience by Month 4 and the budget will not renew.

options.label: *"Cost-per-seat reduction at renewal. If we can renegotiate down 30%, we win."*
options.explain: That's the Bengaluru SaaS outcome, sold as a victory. Lower cost on shelfware is still shelfware. Wrong metric.

options.label: *"Adoption + one outcome metric per function + a quarterly written review of what worked, what didn't, what we're cutting."*
options.explain: **Best answer.** Numbers plus narrative. The quarterly review forces the team to actually *think* about the data, not just stare at a dashboard. That's the difference between a transformation and a tooling line item.

outcomes.perfect: You redirected ₹2 crore from seats to humans, anchored the CTO in evidence, and shipped a metric the CFO can actually use. **Omkar opens his veteran's notebook and writes your name in.** On to Week 14.
outcomes.good: You avoided the headline mistake but flinched on one decision. Re-read the **1:3 tool-to-training ratio** before the next budget meeting.
outcomes.learn: You spent like a procurement manager, not a director. Re-read the lesson — the Bengaluru SaaS firm in your field notes spent ₹1.7 crore for 14% usage. Your draw was a drill. The next ₹2 crore won't be.

points: Every team runs handoff patterns — A (human-only), B (human-first/AI-assist), C (AI-first/human-review) — even when nobody named them.
Trust drifts upward; calibration loops are the only thing that catches it; 2 weeks is the rhythm because that's how confidence creeps.
An AI output is not an artifact; the artifact has one name on it and that person owns it like they typed it.
Tools without training is the most expensive cliché of 2026 — never ship a license without a redesigned ritual.
If you cannot name a workflow's signer in five seconds, you don't have a workflow; you have a leak waiting for a customer.

lessons.title: Hiring for the AI Era
lessons.subtitle: Execution went to zero; judgment is the only thing left to filter on

audioChapters.label: Why your old interview loop is broken
The classic trap and a try-it

blocks.md:
Your hiring loop was designed for an era where execution was the moat. *Can you write the SQL?* *Can you draft the brief?* *Can you build the model?* The candidate who could execute fastest, cleanest, with the most polish, was the candidate to hire. That world ended quietly some time in 2024, and most companies are still running interviews from it.

In 2026 the moat is not 'can you do it', because Claude can do it. The moat is *can you tell when the AI is about to do something stupid, and stop it*. That's a different filter, and it requires a different interview. By the end of this lesson you'll know how to redesign your loop for judgment, and the specific behavioral questions that separate the people who use AI from the people who supervise it.

blocks.title: Mental model: hire for judgment, because execution went to zero
blocks.md:
Hold this picture every time you walk into an interview. Execution skill — the ability to do the well-defined thing well — is now a commodity AI provides. Judgment — the ability to tell when a plausible answer is the wrong answer, when to push back, when to escalate, when to refuse — is the only thing left for a human to be senior at.

The old hiring filter ran on **can you do it?** The new filter runs on **can you tell when it's wrong?** Most candidates can do it, because Claude can do it. Far fewer can spot the error in a 1,800-word draft that reads beautifully. That's the bar. Build the loop around that bar.

hi-IN.title: IIT topper vs the senior who reads line 47
hi-IN.md:
Bhai, ek interview real story. IIT-Delhi 2025 batch, 9.4 CGPA, ChatGPT pe sab kuch *one-shot* solve karta hai. Same panel mein, NIT-Trichy 2017 batch, 8 saal ka veteran. AI ka draft dekhta hai aur 11th line pe ruk gaya — *"This number doesn't match the source. Where did this come from?"*

Fresher confidence se bola — *"Isn't important sir, AI gave it."* Veteran chuppchap source check kara, number galat tha. Kis ko hire kara? Veteran ko. Kyun? Execution AI deta hai. Line 47 read karna seekhna 8 saal lagte hain.

en.title: Same role, two candidates
en.md: Real story. The fresh IIT graduate with the 9.4 CGPA can one-shot every coding task with Claude. The senior with eight years of experience pauses at line 11 of the AI's draft and asks, *'where did this number come from?'* The number turned out to be hallucinated. Both could execute; one of them could supervise. Hire the supervisor. Execution is what AI gives you for free. Reading line 47 takes years.

blocks.caption: Watch (~30s) · Decisions that move to AI; decisions that don't — 6 decision types.

blocks.md:
The classical T-shape was a hiring metaphor invented at IDEO and spread across every tech company in the 2010s: broad surface knowledge across many areas, with deep expertise in one. It's still useful — but the *what* of the depth has changed. In 2026 the depth bar is **judgment in one specific domain**, supported by a thin connecting band of **AI-orchestration skill** that bridges the broad top and the deep bottom.

Three numbers worth carrying. Roughly **40% of mid-level execution work is now done by AI** in companies that have actually redesigned (most haven't). About **15% of senior judgment work** has moved to AI assistance, but the responsibility remains human. Less than **3% of strategic ambiguity arbitration** is AI-touched at all. The implication for hiring: the squeeze is in the middle. Mid-level roles defined purely by execution are evaporating; senior roles defined by judgment are *more* valuable than they were three years ago, because there are fewer people who can supervise the new junior — Claude.

The leadership move is to rewrite your job descriptions around judgment in a specific domain, with AI-orchestration as a stated competency rather than a buzzword. *'5 years of experience'* is a lazy proxy. *'Has caught at least three plausible-but-wrong AI outputs in production work, and can describe the failure mode'* is a real filter.

blocks.title: Translation: 'we need a senior PM' to a hiring rubric that filters for judgment

steps.label: Step 1 — Name the judgment moments
steps.body: List 5 decisions a senior PM on this team made last quarter that an AI would not have made well. Be specific: 'said no to the founder's pet feature', 'caught the wrong dashboard metric before launch', 'pulled a deadline because engineering was hiding burnout'.

steps.label: Step 2 — Convert each into a behavioral question
steps.body: Each judgment moment becomes a 'tell me about a time' question. Avoid hypotheticals — those reward articulate liars. Past behavior is the only signal that ports.

steps.label: Step 3 — Define the AI-supervisor probe
steps.body: One question: 'Tell me about a time AI gave you a confident answer that turned out to be wrong. How did you catch it?' If they cannot answer, they have not actually used AI as a senior; they've used it as a junior.

steps.label: Step 4 — Define the restraint probe
steps.body: One question: 'Walk me through a decision where you chose not to use AI even though you could have.' The strongest seniors say no to AI sometimes. Those who never have, haven't been supervising it.

steps.label: Step 5 — Set the rubric, calibrate the panel
steps.body: Three levels per question: clear example with the failure mode named (4 points); plausible example without specifics (2 points); vague or absent (0 points). Calibrate the panel against three real candidates from the past quarter so the bar isn't drifting.

blocks.prompt: You're hiring a Senior Data Analyst. Which of these is the strongest single filter for the AI-era role?

choices.label: Can describe a real instance where they caught an AI hallucinated number before it shipped, and the failure mode it represented
choices.explain: Correct. This proves they read line 47, they understand failure modes, and they have actually supervised AI output in real work. The other filters are weaker proxies.

choices.label: Lists 14 AI tools on their resume
choices.explain: Tool fluency is a vanity metric. The AI-fluent label tells you nothing about whether they can spot a wrong answer.

choices.label: Has the highest SQL-test score from the take-home
choices.explain: SQL execution is exactly the skill AI commoditised. High score on a take-home in 2026 mostly tells you they used Claude well.

choices.label: Comes from a brand-name company
choices.explain: Brand correlates with confidence, not with judgment about AI failure modes. Many big-co analysts have never been forced to supervise AI in production.

hi-IN.title: Resume mein '14 AI tools' likhne wala candidate
hi-IN.md:
Bhai, candidate aaya — *"AI-fluent"*, resume pe Copilot, Cursor, Claude, Gemini, Midjourney, ChatGPT, Replit, Lovable, Bolt, v0, Perplexity, Pi, Glean, Notion AI. *14 tools*.

Interview mein pucha — *"Konse kaam pe AI ne tujhe galat answer diya, aur tune kaise pakda?"* Frozen. Bola — *"Hmm, mujhe dhyaan nahi."* 14 tools, 0 catches. Yeh tool literacy hai, judgment nahi. Filter karne ki cheez yahi hai — tools list nahi, catches list.

en.title: Tool fluency is not judgment
en.md: A candidate's resume lists 14 AI tools as proof of being 'AI-fluent'. In the interview you ask, *'tell me about a time AI gave you a confident wrong answer and how you caught it.'* They freeze. Fourteen tools, zero catches. The list signals literacy, not judgment. The filter you actually want is the catches list, and most candidates don't have one because they have not yet been forced to supervise rather than to use.

blocks.caption: Watch (~30s) · The cost of a wrong AI decision — 1 mis-route, 12 cascade effects.

blocks.md:
Behavioral interviews work because past specific behavior predicts future behavior much better than hypothetical questions. *'Tell me about a time'* > *'what would you do if'*. The 'if' question rewards articulate fluency, which AI also gives candidates for free during prep. The 'time' question requires a real episode that the candidate has to remember, recount, and defend.

Four questions, used together, cover most of what you need for an AI-era senior role:

1. **The catch**: *Tell me about a time an AI tool gave you a confident answer that turned out to be wrong. How did you notice and what did you change?*
2. **The restraint**: *Walk me through a decision where you chose not to use AI even though you could have. Why?*
3. **The hand-off**: *Describe a workflow you redesigned to use AI. Who owns the artifact, who reviews, what's the failure mode?*
4. **The disagreement**: *Tell me about a time your team wanted to ship something AI produced and you said no. What was the cost and what would you do differently?*

Notice what's missing: questions about model preferences, prompt-engineering tricks, or vendor brand allegiances. Those are the soundbites; the four above are the substance. A candidate who has not been forced to supervise will not have specific stories. They'll generalise. Generalisation is the tell.

intro: Same Vidya. We're now in interview-signal territory.

I'll give you 6 candidate answers to AI-era behavioral questions. Tell me — is this a **strong signal** (specific + failure mode named), **weak signal** (generic or self-promoting), or a **red flag** (suggests they don't actually supervise AI)?
Some of these are real answers from interviews I sat on. Others I made up. You won't be able to tell which is which, and that's the point.

scenarios.situation: Q: 'Tell me about a time AI gave you a confident wrong answer.' A: 'Last March I asked Claude to summarise a 14-page MSA for our biggest client. It confidently said the renewal cap was 7%. The actual clause was 12%. I caught it because I always cross-check renewal numbers against the PDF. Cost would have been ~₹40 lakh on a 4-year contract if I'd taken it at face value.'
scenarios.explain: Specific date, specific document, exact failure mode (number hallucination on a contract term), specific cost. This is the textbook strong signal.

scenarios.situation: Q: 'Tell me about a time AI gave you a confident wrong answer.' A: 'Oh, AI gets things wrong all the time. You always have to verify. I'm very careful about that.'
scenarios.explain: Pure generality. No date, no domain, no specific failure mode. They've heard the right answer; they haven't lived it.

scenarios.situation: Q: 'Walk me through a decision where you chose NOT to use AI.' A: 'When I'm firing someone, I write the message myself. AI sounds plausible but it can't carry the relationship history with this specific person, and the words have to be mine when they ask why later.'
scenarios.explain: Names the calibration issue (relationship history), names the accountability issue (the words have to be mine). This is the restraint signal you want.

scenarios.situation: Q: 'Walk me through a decision where you chose NOT to use AI.' A: 'I always use AI. Why would you not? It's faster.'
scenarios.explain: Red flag. Either they have not been forced to supervise AI in a high-stakes setting, or they have and they didn't notice. Either way they will not be a senior who catches your team's mistakes.

scenarios.situation: Q: 'Describe a workflow you redesigned to use AI.' A: 'I rolled out ChatGPT to my team last year. They love it. Productivity is way up.'
scenarios.explain: No artifact owner, no failure mode, no calibration loop, no specific workflow. They rolled out a tool, not a workflow. Probe further before deciding, but the default reading is weak.

scenarios.situation: Q: 'Tell me about a time your team wanted to ship something AI produced and you said no.' A: 'Two months ago, my analyst sent me an AI-generated competitor analysis with a confident claim that Razorpay had 38% market share. The number was a hallucination. I held the deck, made him source every claim, and we found three more. Took an extra day; saved a meeting with the CEO that would have torched our credibility.'
scenarios.explain: Recent date, specific number, named the failure mode (number hallucination), named the cost of not catching it (CEO meeting credibility). Promote this person if they're internal; hire fast if they're not.

blocks.caption: Watch the trap happen live — and the fix at the end.

blocks.title: The classic trap: hire for AI fluency, not for the actual job
blocks.md:
The most common 2026 hiring mistake: a candidate's resume looks like an AI tool buffet, the recruiter is impressed, and the interview drifts into 'how do you use Cursor/Claude/Copilot' territory. Two rounds later, you've hired someone who can talk about AI but cannot actually do product strategy, financial analysis, or whatever the role is supposed to do.

AI fluency is necessary but not sufficient. The role is *senior product manager* or *senior data analyst* or *senior content lead*. Filter on the job's actual outcomes first; treat AI as a means, not the end. If you can't tell a candidate's AI fluency story apart from someone who watched 4 YouTube videos, that's the problem to solve. The four behavioral questions above are the cheapest fix.

blocks.instruction: Pick a senior role you'll hire for in the next 90 days. Write 4 behavioral questions calibrated for AI-era judgment. For each, write a one-line description of what a 'strong signal' answer would contain.
blocks.starter:
Role: <title>

Q1 (the catch): <question>
Strong signal looks like: <one-line description>

Q2 (the restraint): <question>
Strong signal: <description>

Q3 (the hand-off): <question>
Strong signal: <description>

Q4 (the disagreement): <question>
Strong signal: <description>
blocks.expected:
Role: Senior Marketing Manager (B2B SaaS, India)

Q1 (the catch): 'Tell me about a time an AI tool produced a piece of marketing content with a confident claim that turned out to be wrong. How did you catch it and what did you change about your process afterwards?'
Strong signal looks like: A specific piece of content, a specific factual error (number, citation, competitor reference), and a named workflow change (added a fact-check step, hired a junior to spotcheck, etc.).

Q2 (the restraint): 'Walk me through a piece of customer-facing content where you chose to write it yourself without AI assistance. Why?'
Strong signal: Names the kind of content where AI output is risky — apologies, sensitive announcements, anything that depends on relationship history with the customer.

Q3 (the hand-off): 'Describe a content workflow on your team where AI now contributes a draft. Who signs the published artifact, what's the review checklist, what's the failure mode you watch for?'
Strong signal: Names a single signer (not a rotation), a checklist under 90 seconds, and a specific failure mode like 'praises competitor by accident' or 'cites a regulation that doesn't exist'.

Q4 (the disagreement): 'Tell me about a time a junior on your team wanted to ship AI-generated content and you said no. What was the cost of saying no, and what would you do differently?'
Strong signal: Acknowledges that saying no had a real cost (junior frustrated, deadline missed, etc.) and reflects on the tradeoff rather than self-congratulating.

blocks.prompt: Pick the TWO interview practices most worth retaining in the AI era:

choices.label: Behavioral 'tell me about a time' questions about specific past episodes
choices.explain: Correct. Past specific behavior is the most ports-to-future-behavior signal you have, and it's the hardest to fake with AI prep.

choices.label: Calibrating panels against known past candidates
choices.explain: Correct. Without calibration the bar drifts, especially as AI helps every candidate sound more polished. Calibration is the only way the rubric stays meaningful.

choices.label: Whiteboard SQL or coding tasks the candidate solves alone
choices.explain: Now mostly tests prompt skill. Either let them use AI explicitly, or replace with a judgment task.

choices.label: Long take-home assignments with no time bound
choices.explain: Take-homes were always biased toward those with free time; in 2026 they mostly test how well someone uses Claude.

hi-IN.title: Mummy ka interview test — story bina toh sab vibe hai
hi-IN.md:
Mummy se kabhi pucha — *"Kya aapne kabhi mistake ki?"* Mummy turant specific batayegi — *"1998 mein, navratri ke time, aalu wala sabzi mein bahut zyada haldi daal di thi, papa ne hass-hass ke kha li"*. Date, dish, person, outcome.

Senior candidates ko same test do. Specific story, specific failure mode, specific cost. Agar sirf — *"Yes I learn from mistakes"* type answer aaye, woh corporate vibe hai. Mummy se zyada accountability test pass karna hai.

en.title: The mum-test for behavioral answers
en.md: Ask your mum about a mistake she made and you'll get a date, a dish, a person, and an outcome inside fifteen seconds. Apply the same standard to senior candidates. If their answer to *'tell me about a time'* is closer to 'I always learn from mistakes' than to 'last March, the MSA, the 7% renewal cap', it's corporate vibe, not real episode. Mum-grade specificity is the bar.

blocks.title: Field Notes: The 4,700 Applicants Who Couldn't Ship
blocks.source: Hiring post-mortem at a Mumbai-based fintech (Series D, ~600 employees)
blocks.story:
In June 2025, the head of engineering at a Mumbai fintech rewrote three senior-engineer JDs using ChatGPT and a list of trending terms. The required-skills section now read: *"Demonstrated experience with prompt engineering, RAG architectures, vector databases (Pinecone/Weaviate/Qdrant), agentic frameworks (LangChain/LlamaIndex/AutoGen), embeddings, fine-tuning, and LLMOps."*

The JD was posted on LinkedIn, Naukri, and Instahyre simultaneously. **Within 11 days: 4,712 applications.** The ATS, configured for keyword matching, surfaced 312 "strong matches." Eight made it to onsites. **One was hired** — a candidate whose resume claimed four years of LangChain experience (LangChain was released in October 2022).

The hire was offered ₹68 lakh fixed plus ESOPs. He started in September. **By December he had not shipped a single feature to production.** When asked, in week 14, to explain a tradeoff between two retrieval strategies, he opened ChatGPT in front of the interviewer-now-colleague. The notice period began that afternoon.

The hiring manager's review, written for the new VP-Engineering: *"We hired the resume that matched the JD we wrote. The JD didn't ask for judgement. So we didn't get any."*
blocks.takeaway: Keyword JDs filter for keyword candidates. If you want judgement, write the JD around a problem, not a tool stack.

blocks.title: Boss Battle: The Senior Engineer JD
blocks.setup:
**Week 14.** Rajiv has a senior-engineer slot to fill. Head of Engineering sent over a draft JD this morning — fourteen bullet points, mostly tool names. The recruiter wants to post it by EOD because *"the market moves fast."* Rajiv reads it once, feels uneasy, opens Slack, and pings you.

*"Coach. Five minutes? I think this JD is going to bite us."*

It is 2:14pm. The recruiter's deadline is 6pm. You have one short Zoom.

coach.name: Chief-People-Officer Charumati
coach.role: CPO, 22 years, has read more bad JDs than she'd like to admit

stages.prompt: Charumati shares her screen. *"Rajiv, this draft is fourteen tool names and a salary band. What do you fix first?"*

options.label: Add three more tools to the list — the recruiter says we're behind on "AI-native" hiring keywords.
options.explain: You just made the Mumbai fintech mistake. More keywords means more keyword-matched applicants and zero signal on judgement. Charumati: *"You're optimising for resume volume, not hire quality."*

options.label: Replace the tool list with a one-paragraph problem statement: the actual broken thing this person will own in their first 90 days.
options.explain: **Correct.** A problem-anchored JD filters for people who can think about *that problem*, not people whose resume happens to mention LangChain. Tools change every six months; the problem doesn't.

options.label: Keep the tool list but raise the experience requirement to 8+ years to filter out junior candidates.
options.explain: Years of experience with tools that didn't exist eight years ago is a contradiction. You'll just push the resume-padding from "4 years of LangChain" to "8 years of LangChain" — which is the Mumbai fintech outcome with extra steps.

options.label: Throw the JD away entirely and post nothing — referrals only.
options.explain: Referrals-only on a senior role narrows your pool to your network's pattern, which is usually more of the people you already have. Useful as one channel, not the whole strategy.

stages.prompt: Rajiv asks: *"Okay, problem-anchored. But the recruiter still needs *something* searchable. What goes in the must-haves?"*

options.label: *"Must have shipped at least one production system that real users depend on. We'll ask them to describe it in the screen."*
options.explain: **Yes.** Production experience with stakes is uncopyable on a resume. Anyone can list LangChain; few can describe a 3am pager incident they caused and fixed. Charumati: *"This is how you filter for judgement."*

options.label: *"Must have 5+ years of AI/ML experience."*
options.explain: Five years of "AI/ML" in 2026 means anything from "I ran a Kaggle notebook in 2019" to "I trained foundation models at DeepMind." The phrase has stopped filtering anything.

options.label: *"Must have a Github with 500+ stars on an AI repo."*
options.explain: Stars correlate with marketing skill, not engineering judgement. Plenty of 500-star repos don't run, and plenty of production-grade systems are private.

options.label: *"Must be able to articulate when *not* to use AI for a given problem."*
options.explain: **Brilliant.** Negative-framing skill is rare and load-bearing. The Mumbai fintech hire failed precisely because he couldn't reason about tradeoffs. Add this to the screening question, not the JD bullet.

stages.prompt: JD is rewritten. Recruiter asks: *"How do we screen 500 expected applicants in two weeks?"* Last call.

options.label: *"ATS keyword filter on the new JD's must-haves, then screen the top 50."*
options.explain: You just put a keyword filter on a JD you specifically rewrote to *not* be keyword-driven. Charumati: *"Why did we do the last hour of work then?"*

options.label: *"One-question written submission: 'Describe a system you shipped that broke in production. What did you change in your design afterwards?' Read every answer."*
options.explain: **This is the move.** A 200-word written answer reveals more than 14 keyword bullets ever could. Yes, you read every one. Yes, it takes time. That's the whole point.

options.label: *"Auto-reject anyone whose resume mentions ChatGPT — they're padding."*
options.explain: You'll auto-reject half your real candidates because everyone has used ChatGPT by now. Resume signal is too noisy to use as a filter on its own.

options.label: *"Take-home: build a tiny RAG-over-our-docs prototype in 4 hours. Pay for their time."*
options.explain: **Solid.** A bounded, paid take-home filters for people who can ship under a deadline. Pair it with the written submission and you have two independent signals. Charumati nods. *"Director-grade hiring funnel."*

outcomes.perfect: You replaced a keyword JD with a problem statement, filtered for shipped-it experience, and built a screening funnel that rewards judgement. **Charumati saves the JD as a template.** On to Week 20.
outcomes.good: You avoided the resume-soup outcome but flinched once. Re-read the lesson on **JD-as-problem-statement** before the next req opens.
outcomes.learn: You optimised for application volume and got the Mumbai fintech outcome on paper. Re-read the lesson — that fintech paid ₹68 lakh for a hire who couldn't ship in 14 weeks. The good news: this was a drill.

blocks.caption: Try (~60s) · When AI disagrees with you — 4 disagreements; what do you do?

points: Execution skill went to zero in 2024; judgment is the only thing left for a senior to be filtered on.
The new T-shape is broad-top, AI-orchestration band, deep-judgment-in-one-domain bottom.
The hiring squeeze is in the middle layer; mid-level pure-execution roles evaporate while senior judgment roles get more valuable.
Four behavioral questions cover most of what you need: the catch, the restraint, the hand-off, the disagreement.
'Hire for AI fluency, not the actual job' is the trap that fills your team with people who can talk about AI but cannot do the work.

blocks.prompt: Look at the last senior candidate you rejected. Could you, today, name in one sentence the specific judgment failure mode they couldn't demonstrate? If yes, your loop is working. If no, what's the question you should have asked?

lessons.title: Continuous Learning as a Leadership Move
lessons.subtitle: Weekly demos and public mistakes beat the annual L&D budget every time

audioChapters.label: Why annual L&D produces zero capability
The classic trap and a try-it

blocks.md:
Your L&D budget for 2026 is not actually a learning budget. It is a feel-good budget that produces certificates, attendance reports, and the occasional inspirational PDF. The reason is structural, not motivational: AI capability shifts faster than any annual training cycle can keep up with. By the time the deck is approved, the vendor selected, and the course delivered, the model has had two minor releases and the workflow has changed.

The leadership move is to stop running L&D like a vendor procurement cycle and start running it like a software team runs sprints. Short, specific, owned, with public artifacts. By the end of this lesson you'll have two rituals — the public-mistake protocol and the weekly demo — that, between them, do more for organisational capability than any annual training week your CHRO has ever defended at the budget meeting.

blocks.title: Mental model: learning sprints, not annual L&D budget
blocks.md:
Stop thinking of L&D as a budget you spend once a year. Start thinking of it as a sprint cadence the team runs continuously, like engineering runs two-week sprints. **Short** — one new thing per fortnight, not seven things per quarter. **Specific** — one team's actual workflow, not a generic course catalogue. **Owned** — a named person who runs the demo, not a vendor.

The knowledge half-life on AI tooling is roughly six weeks. That means whatever you train on in February has aged by April, and is dated by August. Annual training cannot keep up. Sprint cadence can. The unit of L&D is no longer a course; it's a 30-minute ritual that happens every two weeks, on the calendar, with an artifact that proves what was learned.

blocks.caption: AI tooling knowledge decays in 6 weeks. Watch what annual training looks like against this clock vs sprint cadence.

hi-IN.title: L&D week ka classic ritual — 4 din, 0 change
hi-IN.md:
Bhai, scene yeh hai. L&D head ne October mein 4-day AI training week organise kara. Ek expensive consultant — *Davos pe spoke*. 800 employees attend kiye, lunch nice tha, certificates LinkedIn pe dale.

November mein puchha — *"Konsa workflow change hua?"* Chuppi. December mein puchha — *"Konsa demo hoga is hafte?"* Demo? Yeh budget item nahi tha. *"Iska baad waala session next March mein hai sir, calendar pe dala hua hai."* March mein pehle session ka content already irrelevant. Yeh L&D nahi hai, yeh attendance hai.

en.title: Four days of training, zero changed workflows
en.md: An L&D head schedules a four-day AI training week in October with an expensive consultant. Eight hundred attend, the lunch is good, certificates go up on LinkedIn. In November you ask which workflow has changed; silence. In December you ask whose demo is on this week; nobody knows what a demo is. The next session is in March. By March the October content is already obsolete. That's not learning; that's attendance.

blocks.caption: Watch (~30s) · What your team is actually scared of — 5 fears, ranked honestly.

blocks.md:
If you only adopt one ritual from this lesson, adopt this one. The **public-mistake protocol** is a 15-minute, dated, recurring slot where a senior person on the team stands up and says: *Last fortnight, I did this with AI. It went wrong like this. Here's what it cost and what I changed.* The senior goes first. Always.

The protocol works because it is the only thing strong enough to overcome the social cost of admitting an AI failure. Junior people will not surface AI mistakes if they think it'll cost them their next review. They will hide them, work around them, and the failure mode will quietly find production through a different path. When the most senior person in the room says *'I did this and it cost ₹4 lakh'* with specifics, the protocol resets the social contract: surfacing mistakes is *the work*, not a confession.

A crisp number from the field: teams that ran this protocol weekly for 12 weeks reported 3.2x more AI failure modes surfaced internally compared to teams that didn't. More importantly, the cost-per-incident dropped because the failure modes were caught at week 2 instead of being discovered by a customer at week 14. The math is straightforward. The cost is the senior's ego. That's the lever.

blocks.title: Translation: 'we should learn from AI mistakes' to a runnable weekly ritual

steps.label: Step 1 — Senior books the slot
steps.body: Calendar: every Friday 4:30pm, 30 minutes, recurring. Senior leader (you) goes first for at least the first 6 weeks. Don't delegate this; if you delegate, you've signalled it's not real.

steps.label: Step 2 — Senior shares first
steps.body: One specific incident. What you did with AI, what went wrong, what it cost (in money or time or trust), what you'll change. Be specific to the point of discomfort. Vague stories signal vague intent.

steps.label: Step 3 — Open the room
steps.body: Two slots for anyone else. First fortnight, nobody volunteers; that's expected. Don't fill the silence; sit in it. Second fortnight, one volunteer. Sixth fortnight, fight for slots.

steps.label: Step 4 — Capture the artifact
steps.body: Each shared mistake gets a 5-line entry in a shared 'Mistakes Wiki' — date, owner, AI tool, failure mode, change made. The wiki is the proof the protocol is compounding. Without it, it's confession; with it, it's curriculum.

steps.label: Step 5 — Reference the wiki in onboarding
steps.body: New hires read the last 8 weeks of mistakes in their first week. This is the fastest way to seed the protocol's norms in someone who joined after you started it. Skip this and the protocol doesn't survive a year of attrition.

blocks.prompt: You're rolling out the public-mistake protocol. Your VP wants to delegate the first session to an L&D manager because 'they run training'. What's the right move?

choices.label: Refuse the delegation; the senior goes first or the protocol does not work — there is no version where someone else carries the social cost on the senior's behalf
choices.explain: Correct. The whole mechanism is the senior's vulnerability resetting the social cost for everyone else. Delegating it to L&D signals 'this is a process to comply with', not 'this is how we work'.

choices.label: Let L&D run it for the first month, senior takes over later
choices.explain: By month two the protocol has been miscoded as a training program rather than a leadership ritual. Recovery is hard.

choices.label: Have L&D and the senior co-host
choices.explain: Splits the signal. The story has to be the senior's own; co-hosting dilutes accountability.

choices.label: Skip the senior demo; just publish a Slack template
choices.explain: A template without a vulnerable example produces zero submissions. The mechanism does not work without the first vulnerable share.

hi-IN.title: Naani ki gallti vs corporate gallti — kis ko surface karna easy hai?
hi-IN.md:
Naani ki kitchen mein, koi sabzi mein zyada namak ho gaya — naani turant batati hai, sab hass-ke khaate hain, next time kam namak. Yeh public-mistake protocol hai, sirf 60 saal pehle se chal raha hai.

Corporate mein koi AI ne galat number bhej diya — kya hota hai? Slack pe quietly delete, fir 'oh no big deal'. Yahi reset karna hai. Senior leader ne pehle apni gallti share kara, junior ka 'safe to share' switch on ho jaata hai. Naani knew this in 1985.

en.title: Why kitchens have a better mistake culture than offices
en.md: In your grandmother's kitchen, when something goes wrong with the salt, she announces it. Everyone laughs, eats anyway, the next batch is better. That is the public-mistake protocol, just sixty years older. In your office when AI ships a wrong number, the message gets quietly deleted and replaced with 'no big deal'. The fix is the same as in the kitchen: the senior shares first. Once that happens, the junior's safe-to-share switch flips. The kitchen has been doing this since 1985.

blocks.caption: Watch (~30s) · The all-hands that goes wrong — 3 announcement patterns.

blocks.md:
The second move pairs cleanly with the first: the **weekly demo**. Every Wednesday afternoon, 25 minutes, one team member demos *one new thing they did with AI this week*. Could be a workflow they redesigned, a prompt they iterated, a failure they caught. The demo is the artifact, and the artifact is the proof.

Why weekly? Because the half-life is six weeks and an annual program can't keep up. Why one person? Because rotation is the discipline; everyone gets to host once a quarter, and that creates the implicit pressure to *find* a thing worth demoing. Why 25 minutes? Because anything longer becomes a presentation, and presentations are theatre. Demos are working sessions: open the laptop, show the prompt, show the output, show the change, take three questions, sit down.

The demo cadence does three things at once that no annual training does: it surfaces internal expertise (*Anika's been doing this brilliant thing nobody knew about*); it creates a low-stakes audience for trying new things (*if I have to demo Wednesday, I might as well try the new tool today*); and it converts L&D from a vendor procurement to a peer ritual. Six months in, the demo wiki contains more practical AI knowledge than the slide deck the consultant sold you for ₹14 lakh. The cost is 25 minutes a week. That is the entire investment.

blocks.title: The classic trap: L&D = compliance training
blocks.md:
The most common L&D failure mode in 2026 is treating AI training as a compliance line item. Module assigned, video watched, certificate issued, attendance logged. Compliance is necessary for things like data-handling and harassment policy; it is *useless* for capability building.

The tell: if the only artifact your training produces is a completion record, you're running compliance, not learning. The fix is to switch the artifact. Demos produce wiki entries. Public-mistake protocol produces a mistakes wiki. Sprint cadence produces a workflow change log. These are artifacts that compound; certificates do not. The board may still want certificate counts in a deck — fine, give them that and run the real protocol underneath.

blocks.prompt: Order the 5 steps to launch the weekly-demo ritual on a 30-person team

items.label: Put the recurring calendar slot first
items.detail: Wednesday 4pm, 25 minutes, recurring. Without the slot it never happens. Don't ask permission; book the time and announce.

items.label: Senior leader hosts week 1
items.detail: You demo first. Show your own AI workflow honestly, including the messy bits. This sets what 'demo-grade' means for the team.

items.label: Rotate through the team transparently
items.detail: Everyone gets a slot once per quarter. Publish the rotation. Volunteers fill open slots; mandatory only if needed.

items.label: Capture each demo as a wiki entry
items.detail: 5 lines: presenter, date, what they showed, the failure mode they noticed, what they recommend the team try. The wiki is the proof of compounding.

items.label: Reference the wiki in onboarding for new hires
items.detail: Last 8 weeks of demos in the first-week reading list. Without this the ritual loses meaning every time someone new joins.

blocks.hint: Calendar first, senior demos first, rotate, capture artifacts, seed onboarding.

blocks.instruction: Plan your first 4 weekly demos. Pick the team, name week-1 host (yourself), and write the proposed wiki entry for the demo you'd give. Be specific.
