  - Week 3: Rohan (Content Lead) — calibration loop she runs every 2 weeks
  - Week 4: Priya (Junior AM) — what she tried, what didn't work, what she'd do differently

blocks.prompt: Pick the TWO design choices that make the weekly demo actually compound (rather than become theatre):

choices.label: A wiki entry produced for every demo, with a specific failure mode named
choices.explain: Correct. The artifact is the proof of compounding. Without it, the demo evaporates the moment the meeting ends.

choices.label: Senior leader hosts the first demo personally
choices.explain: Correct. The senior's first demo sets the bar for what 'demo-grade' means and the social permission for honest content. Skip this and you get presentations.

choices.label: Make attendance mandatory with a tracker
choices.explain: Mandatory attendance produces compliance, not learning. People show up physically and tune out mentally.

choices.label: Quarterly external speaker instead of internal hosts
choices.explain: External speakers don't know your workflows. The compounding comes from peer-to-peer transfer of specifics.

hi-IN.title: L&D budget vs cricket coaching — kahan compounding hai?
hi-IN.md:
Bhai, sochna. Indian cricket academy mein roz net practice hoti hai. 25 minutes batting, 25 minutes bowling, har din. Coach standing wahin. *Annual cricket camp* ka koi concept nahi.

L&D mein same logic chalegi. Roz nahi, but har Wednesday. 25 minutes. Ek senior demo de raha hai, sab dekh rahe hain. Net practice. Yeh compounding deta hai. Annual L&D? Yeh ek-week ki Davos trip hai jisme certificate milta hai aur skill nahi.

en.title: Net-practice cadence beats Davos cadence
en.md: An Indian cricket academy runs 25 minutes of batting and 25 of bowling every single day. There is no 'annual cricket camp' that produces test players. L&D works on the same logic. Not every day, but every week, with the senior present. The annual L&D week is a Davos trip with certificates; the demo cadence is net practice with compounding.

blocks.title: Field Notes: Four Hours, Three Incidents
blocks.source: L&D audit at a 500-person services firm, Pune (financial services vertical)
blocks.story:
On April 8, 2025, the Chief People Officer of a 500-person Pune services firm rolled out a **mandatory annual 4-hour AI ethics training**. The format: a vendor-built e-learning module with seven scenarios, three quizzes, and a printable certificate. Completion was tied to the December performance cycle. By July, **98% completion**. The CPO had a slide for the board.

Between August 2025 and February 2026 the firm had **three AI-related incidents** that triggered internal review:

1. **August** — a senior consultant pasted a client's redacted-but-not-quite contract into ChatGPT to summarise it. Client name was in the metadata.
2. **November** — a manager used an AI tool to draft a performance improvement plan and forgot to remove the placeholder *"[insert weakness here]"* before sending.
3. **February** — a partner shared a board-deck draft, generated by an internal RAG tool, that hallucinated a competitor revenue number; it almost shipped to the actual board.

All three incident-causers had completed the 4-hour training. All three certificates were on file. The post-mortem, written by the new VP-People, contained one sentence in bold: *"Annual training does not change weekly behaviour."* The 2026 plan replaced the e-learning module with **weekly 20-minute team sprints**, owned by line managers, with one recent real-world scenario per week. Six months in: zero incidents.
blocks.takeaway: Once-a-year training tests *memory*. Weekly sprints change *habits*. AI risk is a habits problem, so train like it.

blocks.title: Boss Battle: The Annual vs. Weekly Decision
blocks.setup:
**Week 20.** The HR Head, Sneha, just emailed Rajiv a shiny one-pager: *"Annual AI Ethics & Safety Training Programme — 4 hours, vendor-led, mandatory, perfect for the December cycle."* The vendor quote is ₹38 lakh. Sneha has already shown the deck to two partners.

Rajiv pings you.

*"Coach, this is exactly what the field-note Pune firm did. But Sneha's already half-sold to the partners. How do I redirect this without making her look bad?"*

coach.name: Org-Design-Veteran Omkar
coach.role: Org-design veteran, has watched seven annual training programmes fail before lunch

stages.prompt: Omkar leans back. *"Rajiv, the partners are already reading Sneha's deck. What's your opening move?"*

options.label: Approve the annual training. It's mandatory anyway, ticks the compliance box, and we can layer something better on top later.
options.explain: *"Layer something on later"* is how organisations end up with mandatory training *and* no behaviour change. The Pune firm had 98% completion and three incidents. Compliance and effectiveness are different problems.

options.label: Propose a hybrid: keep a 90-minute annual *baseline* for compliance, replace the rest with weekly 20-minute team sprints owned by line managers.
options.explain: **Correct.** You preserve Sneha's compliance need *and* fix the behaviour-change gap. Omkar: *"You gave her a win and the firm a better outcome. That's how you redirect without burning a peer."*

options.label: Kill the annual training entirely. It's bad and we should say so.
options.explain: You'd be technically right and politically dead by the next partner meeting. Sneha walks out, the partners side with her, and your weekly-sprint idea never sees the light. Right answer, wrong delivery.

options.label: Buy two annual programmes — one ethics, one safety — to be extra thorough.
options.explain: Twice the certificates, same zero behaviour change. The Pune firm's three incidents wouldn't have been prevented by adding a fourth hour.

stages.prompt: Sneha agrees to the hybrid. She asks: *"Who runs the weekly sprints? L&D doesn't have bandwidth."* What do you tell Rajiv?

options.label: *"Hire an L&D vendor to deliver weekly sessions across all teams."*
options.explain: Vendor-delivered weekly sessions are just the annual programme served fifty-two times. The whole point is to embed in *team* context. Outsourcing the delivery defeats the design.

options.label: *"Line managers run them. 20 minutes of one real recent scenario, in the team's stand-up slot. L&D supplies the scenario library and a one-page facilitation guide."*
options.explain: **Yes.** Manager-led, in-context, scenario-driven. The team talks about *their* near-misses, not a vendor's hypotheticals. Omkar: *"Now you've turned every manager into an L&D channel. That's leverage."*

options.label: *"Make it self-paced — drop a 20-minute video in Slack every Monday and trust people to watch."*
options.explain: Self-paced video in Slack is the annual programme served as a podcast. No discussion, no team context, no behaviour change. People will mark it watched and scroll.

options.label: *"Run a peer-champion model — three trained champions per function, rotating who facilitates."*
options.explain: **Solid alternative.** Champions scale better than managers in firms where managers are stretched thin. Either model works as long as the *facilitation is local*. Pair with manager support and you're set.

stages.prompt: The CPO asks: *"How do I prove to the board this is working better than the old programme?"* Last call.

options.label: *"Completion rates. Just like before. We'll see 80%+ across teams."*
options.explain: Completion was 98% at the Pune firm. The board needs to see *behaviour* change, not attendance. Wrong metric.

options.label: *"Two metrics: incident count (lagging) and self-reported near-misses (leading). Plus a quarterly anonymous survey on confidence in handling AI scenarios."*
options.explain: **This is the move.** Lagging plus leading plus qualitative. Near-misses-reported is the gold metric — it goes *up* when training is working, because people are noticing more, not because more is going wrong. Omkar saves this in his notebook.

options.label: *"Vibes. Walk the floor, ask people what they did differently this month."*
options.explain: Walking the floor is *necessary* but not sufficient. The board needs a number. "Vibes" is what gets cut when budgets tighten.

options.label: *"Cost-per-employee training spend. Should drop 60% versus the annual programme."*
options.explain: Saving money on training is not the win. The Pune firm saved nothing and spent ₹38 lakh; the new programme will cost less *and* work better. But the board cares about outcomes, not unit costs.

outcomes.perfect: You preserved Sneha's compliance baseline, redirected the bulk into weekly team sprints, and shipped a metric that actually measures behaviour. **Omkar nods slowly. That's the correct nod.** On to Week 26.
outcomes.good: You avoided the once-a-year-tick-the-box outcome but flinched once. Re-read the lesson on **annual vs. weekly cadence** before the next L&D budget cycle.
outcomes.learn: You optimised for compliance and got the Pune firm's three incidents on paper. Re-read the lesson — 98% completion did not stop a single incident there. Your draw was a drill.

points: AI tooling has a 6-week knowledge half-life; annual L&D cycles cannot keep up by design.
Sprint L&D produces capability above a steady-state line; annual training spikes once and decays.
Public-mistake protocol works only when the senior goes first; delegating to L&D destroys the mechanism.
Weekly 25-minute demos with wiki artifacts compound faster than any external training your CHRO will buy.
If the only artifact your L&D produces is a completion certificate, you're running compliance, not learning.

lessons.title: Ethics, Trust, and the Boring Hard Work
lessons.subtitle: Behavior compounds. Posters don't.

audioChapters.label: Opening — the values poster on the wall

blocks.md:
Almost every Indian company has a values poster on the wall. Almost none of those posters predict any behavior. Trust is built (or broken) by what leaders *do* in the small, awkward moments — not by what's typeset above the elevator.

This lesson is the boring hard work: post-mortems, explicit ladders, and the reason values get printed in the first place.

blocks.title: Mental model: behavior compounds, posters don't
blocks.md:
Trust is a compounding asset. Every honest, slightly-uncomfortable disclosure adds. Every small cover-up subtracts. The compound rate is much faster than people expect.

A single public post-mortem of a real near-miss does more for org trust than 47 'lunch and learn' values sessions. It's costly to the leader; that's exactly why it works as a signal.

hi-IN.title: All-hands ke speech vs. corridor ka behavior
hi-IN.md: Indian companies mein all-hands speeches mein 'integrity' word 14 baar aata hai. Corridor mein, manager ne junior ka kaam apna bola — team ne dekha. **Speech bhul jaata hai, corridor yaad rehta hai.** Posters $0 cost; behavior unbounded cost. Yahin se trust banta hai aur tootta hai.

en.title: Speeches vs corridors
en.md: All-hands speeches use the word 'integrity' often. Corridor behavior — what a manager does when they think no one is watching — is the actual signal. Teams remember corridors, not speeches.

blocks.caption: Watch (~30s) · What stays rare — 6 skills, scarcity-over-time.

blocks.md:
When something goes wrong on your watch, you have three options:

1. Cover it up. Hope no one notices. (Trust compound: -2% / week.)
2. Acknowledge privately, fix quietly. (Trust compound: 0%.)
3. **Public post-mortem.** What went wrong, what you missed, what changes structurally. (Trust compound: +3-7% per incident.)

The third option costs you in the short term and pays you in the long term. It's also the rarest. That's why it works as a signal.

blocks.title: Translation moment: 'we shipped a feature that mishandled user data for 4 hours'

steps.label: Day 0 — the incident
steps.body: Feature shipped. Bug discovered. Some users affected. The clock starts.

steps.label: Hour 4 — internal triage
steps.body: Engineering rolls back. Damage assessed. The blame instinct kicks in.

steps.label: Hour 8 — choice point
steps.body: Cover up? Quiet fix? Public post-mortem? Most leaders default to option 2 because it 'feels balanced'. The team sees option 2 as option 1 in a smaller font.

steps.label: Day 1-2 — write the post-mortem
steps.body: What happened, why we missed it (without scapegoating), what changes structurally (eval, review process, incident playbook). Specific. No 'we will be more careful.'

steps.label: Day 3 — share publicly
steps.body: All-hands or written form. Acknowledge the harm to users. Walk through the fix. Take questions. The discomfort is the cost; the trust is the return.

blocks.prompt: What's the trust impact of a public post-mortem on a real incident, vs covering it up?

choices.label: Public post-mortem builds trust over time; cover-ups erode it slowly but compound to a much larger loss
choices.explain: Correct. The asymmetry is what most leaders underestimate. Discomfort is short; the compounding is long.

choices.label: They're roughly equivalent if no one notices the cover-up
choices.explain: Cover-ups are noticed eventually; the team always reads behavior. The 'no one notices' assumption is the trap.

choices.label: Public post-mortems destroy trust because they advertise weakness
choices.explain: Inverse of the truth. Pre-committed transparency builds trust; concealed weakness destroys it.

choices.label: The trust impact is symbolic; what matters is the technical fix
choices.explain: Technical fix matters but the trust impact is real and measurable. Both matter; trust compounds longer.

hi-IN.title: Indian context — 'log kya kahenge' ka counter
hi-IN.md: *"Public post-mortem mein log judge karenge"* — yes, they will. **Lekin woh log already judge kar rahe hain, sirf data ke saath ya bina.** Public post-mortem mein tu data control karta hai, gossip nahi. Indian corporate culture mein 'face-saving' ka cost trust se zyada hai.

en.title: Face-saving costs trust
en.md: The 'people will judge me' instinct is real. But people are already judging — they just don't have the data. A public post-mortem gives you control of the narrative; concealment gives them control via gossip.

blocks.caption: Watch (~30s) · Your skill stack, refactored — where to invest the next 12 mo.

blocks.md:
Most ethics fights at work are not 'is X right or wrong?'. They're *'who decides whether X is right or wrong, and how does that decision get made?'*

The **explicit ladder** is a written, before-the-incident document that says:
- These decisions are made by individual contributors.
- These by managers.
- These by directors.
- These by VPs.
- These by the CEO.
- These by the board.

When a hard call comes — and it will, especially in AI — everyone already knows whose call it is. Ambiguity is the trap; the ladder is the fix.

intro: Right. Five real escalations from real Indian companies. ⚖️
Tell me **who's call** each one is — IC, Manager, Director, VP, CEO, or Board?
When the ladder is ambiguous, the cost is paid in weeks of escalation. Pick wisely.

scenarios.situation: Engineer wants to use Claude Sonnet 4.6 instead of GPT for a feature; cost diff +12%, quality diff +6%.
scenarios.explain: IC call. Tool choice within an existing capability budget is the IC's. Escalating wastes everyone's time.

scenarios.situation: Manager wants to reorganize her 8-person team into two pods of 4. Same heads, same budget.
scenarios.explain: Manager call. Same budget, same heads, structural change within their span. Loop the director for visibility, but it's the manager's call.

scenarios.situation: Director wants to lay off 30% of her org because AI automated their work; CEO and CFO not yet aware.
scenarios.explain: VP / CEO call. Layoffs of this size cross legal, financial, PR, and culture surfaces. Director should propose; VP/CEO decide.

scenarios.situation: CEO wants to pivot the company from B2B SaaS to a B2C AI consumer app; would change everything.
scenarios.explain: Board call. Strategic pivot of this magnitude requires board approval per the company's articles. CEO can propose; board decides.

scenarios.situation: Senior IC wants to publish a research paper that mentions a customer's name. Customer hasn't approved.
scenarios.explain: Director call. Crosses legal/customer surface; IC and manager don't have authority to commit the company externally. Director or VP signs off after legal review.

blocks.title: The classic trap: ambiguous decision rights
blocks.md:
Most 'ethics issues' at work are decision-rights issues in disguise.

A director makes a call that should have been a VP's; six months later it surfaces and the VP is angry. *"Why didn't you tell me?"* — the director didn't know they had to. The fix is not 'be more careful'; the fix is *write the ladder down before the next incident*.

A written ladder, reviewed annually, is one of the highest-trust documents an org can produce. Most don't have one. That's the gap.

blocks.instruction: Pick one decision rights ambiguity that has caused friction on your team. Write the proposed ladder entry: who decides, who's consulted, who's informed (RACI is fine). Make it specific enough that the next time this comes up, no one has to escalate to find out.
blocks.expected:
Decision: 'Switching customer-facing AI feature from one model provider to another.'

- **Decides (R):** Director of Product (cost > ₹5L/month surfaces).
- **Approves (A):** VP Engineering (technical viability + risk).
- **Consulted (C):** Senior eng lead, legal (data residency), security (data flow).
- **Informed (I):** CFO, CMO, customer success lead.

Review cadence: every 6 months at the quarterly ops review. Stored at /docs/decision-ladder.md.

blocks.title: Field Notes: The Audit Log That Outed the Cover-Up
blocks.source: Anonymised internal review at a 1,200-person Indian services firm
blocks.story:
In April 2025, a senior leader at a 1,200-person Indian services firm — a Vice President with eleven years at the company — made a decision the team would later call *"the small lie that cost us four quarters."*

A junior analyst had used the firm's internal AI tool to draft a client recommendation. The tool, fine-tuned on internal data, had hallucinated a regulatory citation. The draft went into a deliverable. A junior on the client's side caught it before it became a public problem. Near-miss. No external damage.

The VP's first instinct was to handle it quietly. He told the analyst to revise the deliverable, asked the client lead to *"smooth it over,"* and made no internal report. He believed — reasonably, in a previous era — that visibility would damage the team's standing.

What the VP did not realise: **the AI tool's audit log was visible to a six-person internal-controls team**, including the junior's prompt, the hallucinated citation, the revision history, and the timestamps. Within two weeks, four people on the team had figured out what happened. Within four weeks, the rest of the team had. Nobody escalated, but the trust map of the team rearranged itself in silence.

In the next anonymous engagement survey, the team's score on *"my leader handles mistakes openly"* dropped from 4.3 to 2.7 out of 5. Two senior associates left. **It took four full quarters of consistent, public post-mortem behaviour from the VP — and one written apology to the team — to bring the score back above 4.0.**
blocks.takeaway: AI tools come with audit logs. The logs are visible to more people than you think. The cost of the cover-up is now always higher than the cost of the truth.

blocks.title: Boss Battle: The Customer Near-Miss
blocks.setup:
**Week 26.** Final week of the six-month transformation. Yesterday afternoon, Rajiv's team had a near-miss: an AI-drafted client deliverable contained a fabricated case-study reference. A junior on Rajiv's side caught it three hours before it shipped. The client never saw the bad version. No revenue at risk. No regulatory exposure.

It is now 8:14am the next morning. Rajiv has a 9:30am team stand-up. The audit log of the incident is visible to the internal-controls team and to two senior partners. Rajiv pings you.

*"Coach. Last call of the six months. Do I post-mortem this publicly or quietly fix it and move on?"*

coach.name: Chief-People-Officer Charumati
coach.role: CPO, has watched more cover-ups outed than confessed

stages.prompt: Charumati's video clicks on. *"Rajiv, you have eighty minutes. What's the call?"*

options.label: Quiet fix. The client never saw it, no harm done, no need to alarm the team or the partners.
options.explain: You just walked into the field-note VP's mistake. The audit log already tells the story to six controls people and two partners. Your team will learn from *them*, not from you, and that's where trust dies.

options.label: Public post-mortem at 9:30am stand-up. Specific facts, specific lessons, no blame on the analyst. Email the partners *before* stand-up.
options.explain: **Correct.** Charumati: *"You're getting ahead of the audit log. The team learns the story from you, the partners hear it from you first, and the analyst gets visible coverage from their leader."*

options.label: Tell the analyst to publicly post-mortem it themselves at stand-up.
options.explain: You outsourced the hard part. The analyst delivers the bad news, the team sees the leader stayed quiet, and the trust signal points the wrong way. Junior people post-mortem their own work; leaders post-mortem the *system that allowed it*.

options.label: Schedule a written post-mortem in next week's all-hands — gives time to prepare a clean narrative.
options.explain: Seven days is enough time for the audit-log story to spread through six conversations. By the time you post-mortem, you're confirming what people already think. Speed matters more than polish.

stages.prompt: Rajiv agrees on the public post-mortem. *"What goes in it?"* What do you tell him?

options.label: *"What happened, what almost happened, what we changed in the process, and one thing I (Rajiv) personally got wrong about how we set this up."*
options.explain: **Yes.** The fourth element — *what the leader got wrong* — is the load-bearing piece. It tells the team that admitting error is safe at every level. Charumati: *"Without that fourth element, this is a memo, not a post-mortem."*

options.label: *"Just the facts and the process change. Don't make it personal."*
options.explain: *"Don't make it personal"* is what people say when they don't want to admit anything. The team is watching whether you take any of the weight. If you don't, the analyst will, and you've thrown them under a bus dressed in process language.

options.label: *"Name and credit the junior who caught it. Then the facts. Then the system fix."*
options.explain: **Excellent.** Naming the catcher publicly does three things: rewards vigilance, shifts the narrative from blame to detection, and signals that catching errors is high-status. Pair this with the *what-I-got-wrong* point and you have a model post-mortem.

options.label: *"Detailed root-cause analysis, including who clicked what and when."*
options.explain: Detailed individual-action attribution turns a post-mortem into a public review. The team will read it as a warning, not a lesson, and people will hide their next near-miss instead of flagging it.

stages.prompt: Stand-up is in twenty minutes. The senior partner pings: *"Rajiv, do we really need to broadcast this? The client doesn't even know."* Last call of the course.

options.label: *"You're right, partner. Let's keep it internal-leadership only and brief the team on the process change without naming the incident."*
options.explain: You folded at the goal line. The audit log is already visible to controls and to *another partner*. The team will piece it together, and now you're also visibly siding with the cover-up. Worst possible ending.

options.label: *"Six people on the controls team and two partners can already see the audit log. The story will be told this week with or without us. Better that it's told by us, with the lessons we want emphasised."*
options.explain: **This is the answer.** You explained the *real* threat model — modern audit infrastructure makes cover-ups expensive — without lecturing the partner. Charumati: *"Now you sound like a Chief Transformation Officer, not a director."*

options.label: *"I hear you, but I've already decided. Standing up at 9:30."*
options.explain: Right call, wrong delivery. *"I've already decided"* tells the partner you don't see them as a thinking participant. You'll get the post-mortem out and lose a useful ally for Quarter 2.

options.label: *"Let me write it up first and send it to you for review. We can decide the audience after."*
options.explain: Once it goes for review, the post-mortem becomes a comms artifact. Stand-up will pass without it. By next stand-up, the audit-log conversation has done its quiet damage. Velocity is the point.

outcomes.perfect: You ran toward the truth, named the catcher, owned a piece of the system error, and held the partner without burning him. **Charumati closes her laptop and says: *"Six months ago you needed me. Now you don't. Go."** End of transformation. Beginning of leadership.
outcomes.good: You avoided the cover-up but flinched once. Re-read the lesson on **public post-mortems** — every quiet fix in the era of audit logs is a slow trust drain.
outcomes.learn: You took the field-note VP's path and traded a small lie for four quarters of damage. Re-read the lesson — modern AI tooling makes cover-ups not just unethical but operationally expensive. Your draw was a drill. The next near-miss won't be.

assessment.title: Leadership in the Age of AI Assessment
assessment.description: Tests whether you can think at the task level, design human-AI handoffs that don't drift, hire for judgment, run L&D as a weekly habit, and tell the difference between a values poster and an actual behavior change.

questions.stem: Your CEO declares 'we are an AI-first company now'. Six months later, every team has a Claude license but nobody has changed how they work. What is the first thing you should diagnose?

choices.label: Nobody redesigned a single team's daily ritual; tools were given but tasks were not relabeled
choices.explanation: Correct. AI changes tasks, not jobs. If the standup, the review, and the handoff still look the same as last year, no transformation has happened. Licenses are the cheap part.

choices.label: The CEO did not pick a strong enough model
choices.explanation: Tempting but wrong. Even the best model produces the same nothing if no team's process changed.

choices.label: People are resistant to change and need motivation
choices.explanation: Resistance is downstream of unclear asks. Nobody knows what they are supposed to do differently on Tuesday. That is a leadership failure, not a motivation failure.

choices.label: The training budget was too small
choices.explanation: Budget is the second-order question. The first-order question is whether anyone changed a single workflow.

questions.stem: Roughly what fraction of knowledge-work tasks are 80%-or-more automatable, versus what fraction of jobs are 0% automatable?

choices.label: About 47% of tasks; about 80% of jobs are 0% automatable
choices.explanation: Correct. The task layer moves fast; the job layer barely budges in the same window. This is why 'automate everyone' is the wrong frame.

choices.label: About 80% of tasks; about 80% of jobs
choices.explanation: If both numbers were 80%, half of knowledge work would already be automated. It isn't, because tasks compose into jobs in ways that resist full automation.

choices.label: About 10% of tasks; about 0% of jobs
choices.explanation: Too low on tasks. The task disruption is real and substantial; the job disruption lags by years.

choices.label: About 100% of both, eventually
choices.explanation: Eventually is not a planning horizon. Lead for the next 18 months, not the long run.

questions.stem: Pick the TWO statements that match the 70-20-10 split for AI-augmented knowledge work in 2026:

choices.label: About 70% of work hours are still purely human (judgment, relationship, ambiguous calls)
choices.explanation: Correct. The boring stuff at the top of the funnel gets compressed; the hard stuff at the bottom does not.

choices.label: About 20% becomes human-with-AI co-work where the artifact is jointly produced
choices.explanation: Correct. This is the largest design challenge: the handoff, the review, the trust calibration.

choices.label: About 70% becomes fully automated end-to-end
choices.explanation: End-to-end automation is rare in knowledge work because the last mile needs context AI does not have.

choices.label: About 50% disappears entirely
choices.explanation: Work shifts; work does not vanish. The mistake is conflating 'task automated' with 'role eliminated'.

questions.stem: A team adds an AI step to their content pipeline. Output volume triples. Three weeks later, three errors slip into a customer-facing email. The team blames Claude. What is the right diagnosis?

choices.label: The trust calibration loop never ran; humans stopped reviewing line by line because the first 200 outputs looked good
choices.explanation: Correct. Trust calibration is the explicit, periodic re-check of where AI fails. Skip it and you discover failure modes through customers, not internal review.

choices.label: Claude got worse over those three weeks
choices.explanation: Models do not silently degrade between releases. The review discipline degraded.

choices.label: The team needed a more expensive model
choices.explanation: Spending more on the same broken loop produces the same errors at higher cost.

choices.label: AI is unsuitable for content work
choices.explanation: Tempting overcorrection. The pipeline did triple output; the failure was in the design of the human checkpoint, not the AI step.

questions.stem: You're designing a human-AI handoff for legal-contract review. Which TWO are essential for the artifact-not-output rule?

choices.label: AI produces a flagged-clause list with citations; the lawyer signs the final memo
choices.explanation: Correct. The lawyer signs an artifact, not Claude's output. AI is upstream of judgment, not the producer of it.

choices.label: Every flag has a 'why' the lawyer can verify in under 90 seconds
choices.explanation: Correct. The artifact rule only works if review is faster than re-doing the work; otherwise the lawyer ignores the AI.

choices.label: Claude's draft is sent directly to the client with a footer disclaimer
choices.explanation: This is the no-review-without-signature failure. The disclaimer protects nobody.

choices.label: The team rotates which lawyer is 'AI-supervisor' each week
choices.explanation: Rotation distributes the failure surface. One owner per artifact, always.

questions.stem: You're hiring a senior product manager. The new T-shape says the depth bar is...

choices.label: Judgment in one specific domain — they can tell when the AI's plausible answer is the wrong one
choices.explanation: Correct. Execution is cheap; spotting a plausible-but-wrong AI plan is the new senior-PM differentiator.

choices.label: Number of frameworks memorised
choices.explanation: Frameworks are now the cheapest part of the job. AI knows more frameworks than your candidate.

choices.label: Speed of typing prompts
choices.explanation: Prompt speed is a 2-week skill. You are hiring for 4-year judgment, not 2-week tooling.

choices.label: Years of experience at FAANG-equivalent companies
choices.explanation: Branded resumes correlate with confidence, not with judgment about AI failure modes.

questions.stem: A candidate's resume says 'AI-fluent' and lists 14 tools. What should this tell you?

choices.label: Almost nothing about whether they can do the actual job; tool fluency is a vanity metric without an outcome attached
choices.explanation: Correct. 'Hire for AI fluency, not the actual job' is the trap. The job is product strategy, or hiring, or growth — AI is a means. Filter on the job's outcomes, then ask 'where did AI help and where did it fail you'.

choices.label: They are clearly the strongest candidate because they are AI-native
choices.explanation: Strong AI-resume signal is also strong 'I copy buzzwords' signal. Test the underlying skill, not the keyword list.

choices.label: They are too junior because they are tooling-focused
choices.explanation: Premature judgment. The list tells you nothing about depth. Run the interview.

choices.label: They will demand a higher salary
choices.explanation: Maybe; irrelevant to whether they can do the job. Decision first, salary second.

questions.stem: Pick TWO behavioral interview questions that probe judgment for an AI-era senior role:

choices.label: 'Tell me about a time AI gave you a confident answer that turned out to be wrong. How did you catch it?'
choices.explanation: Correct. This separates the people who use AI from the people who supervise AI. Anyone senior should have this story.

choices.label: 'Walk me through a decision where you chose not to use AI even though you could have'
choices.explanation: Correct. Restraint is the senior signal. If they have never said no to AI, they have not led with it; they have just adopted it.

choices.label: 'How many tokens did you process last month?'
choices.explanation: Throughput vanity. Tells you nothing about whether the work was good.

choices.label: 'Which AI model do you think is best?'
choices.explanation: Brand loyalty is not skill. Anyone can have a model preference; few can defend a workflow.

questions.stem: Your CEO approves a one-week annual AI training week for all 800 staff. What is the most important thing you should push back on?

choices.label: Annual L&D produces zero behavior change; weekly demos and learning sprints with one new habit per fortnight is the only format that survives
choices.explanation: Correct. Knowledge half-life in AI tooling is roughly six weeks. Annual training is compliance theater. The format must match the rate of change.

choices.label: The week should be two weeks
choices.explanation: Doubling the duration of the wrong format does not fix the format. People forget weekend-2 the same way they forget weekend-1.

choices.label: The trainer should be external
choices.explanation: Internal vs external is a second-order choice. The frequency is the first-order failure.

choices.label: It should be made mandatory with attendance tracking
choices.explanation: Compliance ≠ learning. Mandatory attendance produces certificates, not capability.

questions.stem: Which TWO are core to the public-mistake protocol that makes AI L&D actually compound?

choices.label: Senior leaders share their own AI mistakes first, with specific cost numbers
choices.explanation: Correct. Nothing else creates psychological safety to surface AI failures. If the VP didn't admit one, the AVP won't, and the manager won't, and the cost stays buried.

choices.label: A standing weekly slot where one team demos a failure plus what they changed
choices.explanation: Correct. Weekly cadence and a fixed slot make 'I learned from a mistake' a normal report, not a confession.

choices.label: Performance-management consequences for any AI mistake
choices.explanation: Punishing surfaced mistakes is how you get hidden ones. Fastest path to opaque failures.

choices.label: Annual external training certificates for everyone
choices.explanation: Certificates document attendance, not capability. They do not make mistakes safer to surface.

questions.stem: Your company's 'AI Ethics Committee' has produced a 12-page values document. Six months later, customers are complaining that an automated decision was unfair. The document didn't help. Why?

choices.label: Behavior beats values posters; nobody changed how a single decision was made or escalated
choices.explanation: Correct. Values without behavior changes are PR. The test of an ethics policy is whether one specific Tuesday-morning decision happens differently than it would have without the policy.

choices.label: The document was too short
choices.explanation: Length is not the bug. The 12 pages told nobody what to do at 11 am on a Tuesday when the model output looked off.

choices.label: Customers misunderstand AI
choices.explanation: Blaming the customer is the polite version of blaming the user. The customer noticed; you did not.

choices.label: The committee did not have the right people
choices.explanation: Adjusting committee composition does not change a single behavior on the ground. Behaviors live in workflows, not committees.

questions.stem: Pick TWO things that should be in every transparent failure post-mortem:

choices.label: The exact decision and what AI's role in it was
choices.explanation: Correct. Vague post-mortems ('we'll do better') skip the AI role entirely; that's the part most likely to repeat.

choices.label: One concrete behavior change with an owner and a date
choices.explanation: Correct. Without a behavior change, the post-mortem is decorative. Without an owner and date, the change is decorative.

choices.label: An apology essay from the CEO
choices.explanation: Apologies that are not paired with behavior changes accelerate cynicism.

choices.label: A list of which model was used
choices.explanation: Useful detail but secondary. The model is the actor; the workflow is the system. Fix the system.

questions.stem: The 'explicit ladder' for AI-aided decisions defines four levels. Which is the right ordering, lowest to highest oversight?

choices.label: AI-only → AI-with-spotcheck → AI-with-human-signoff → human-only
choices.explanation: Correct. Every AI-touched workflow lives at one of these four rungs. Naming the rung is the entire point; ambiguity is where errors hide.

choices.label: Human-only → AI-only → spotcheck → signoff
choices.explanation: Out of order. The ladder is about how much human oversight is in the loop, not when AI was introduced.

choices.label: AI-only → human-only → AI-with-signoff → spotcheck
choices.explanation: Random ordering. The point of the ladder is the gradient, not a list.

choices.label: There is no ladder; teams should just use judgment
choices.explanation: Refusing to name the rungs is how you end up with five teams operating at four different rungs and nobody knowing.

questions.stem: You're about to launch an AI-augmented hiring tool. Pick the strongest first move:

choices.label: Pilot on one role family for 60 days, sample 100% of decisions for human review, measure adverse-impact ratio against the prior baseline
choices.explanation: Correct. Hiring is high-stakes, regulated, and reputational. A bounded pilot with full sampling is the only responsible first move.

choices.label: Roll it out to all 14 role families to learn faster
choices.explanation: Faster is not better when the failure mode is bias propagation. Bounded scope first.

choices.label: Run it shadow-mode forever and never decide
choices.explanation: The other failure mode: pilots that never end. Define the decision date in advance.

choices.label: Skip the pilot because the vendor demoed it well
choices.explanation: Vendor demos are sales; pilots are evidence. Never substitute one for the other on something this consequential.

questions.stem: Pick the TWO strongest signals that an 'AI transformation' is theater rather than real:

choices.label: Six months in, no team's daily standup or weekly review has changed
choices.explanation: Correct. Real transformation lives in rituals; if the rituals are unchanged, nothing has changed regardless of slide decks.

choices.label: Leadership cannot name a single workflow that runs differently than it did 12 months ago
choices.explanation: Correct. If the leader cannot point to one specific changed workflow, there is no transformation to point at.

choices.label: AI license utilisation is high
choices.explanation: License utilisation is a proxy that's easy to game. People can use AI all day and produce the same output the same way.

choices.label: External press coverage is positive
choices.explanation: Press is a marketing outcome. It tells you nothing about whether work changed.

questions.stem: Your engineering manager says 'AI does 60% of the coding now, so we can cut headcount by 60%'. The strongest pushback is:

choices.label: 60% of coding-tasks ≠ 60% of an engineer's job; specification, review, debugging cascades, and stakeholder calibration are the harder 40% and they grew, not shrank
choices.explanation: Correct. Confusing task automation with role automation is the most expensive mistake an engineering leader can make in 2026. The remaining 40% is what produces working software, and AI made it heavier, not lighter.

choices.label: AI cannot really do 60% of coding
choices.explanation: Denying the task-level shift is dishonest and unhelpful. The argument is about how task share converts to role share.

choices.label: We need to cut 80% to stay competitive
choices.explanation: Doubling down on the same logic error makes it twice as expensive to recover from.

choices.label: Hire more juniors because AI levels the field
choices.explanation: Mid-level squeeze is real, but this isn't the rebuttal to a headcount-cut argument; it is a separate question about pyramid shape.

questions.stem: What is the most useful single number to track for AI-leadership maturity in the first year?

choices.label: Number of team rituals (standup, review, handoff) that have a named, dated change tied to AI
choices.explanation: Correct. Counts a behavior, not a tool, not a perception. A leader who can name 12 changed rituals has done real work; a leader who cannot has not.

choices.label: Number of AI licenses purchased
choices.explanation: Inputs not outputs. Buying licenses is the easy part.

choices.label: Cost saved per quarter
choices.explanation: Tempting but lagging and easy to fudge. Cost-savings without ritual changes is suspect.

choices.label: Survey score for 'AI excitement'
choices.explanation: Sentiment leads nowhere. Excitement at month 1 is uncorrelated with capability at month 12.

project.title: Capstone: A Six-Month Plan to Become an AI-Native Company
project.prompt:
Your CEO catches you outside the lift on a Wednesday afternoon and says:

*"I need a 6-month plan to become an AI-native company. Org changes, training rollout, the works. Have it on my desk by next Friday. Make it real, please. We've already done two of these and nothing changed."*

She's not wrong. The last two attempts were a values poster, an external training week, and a Microsoft Copilot license rollout. Nothing measurably changed. You have her ear for the third try.

Write the plan. It should be the kind of memo you would actually send a CEO who is tired of theater. Specific, defensible, India-anchored where context matters.

Deliver:

1. **Diagnose the last two attempts.** Name what they got wrong using the language of this course (task vs job confusion, license without ritual change, annual L&D, values without behavior, etc.). Two paragraphs.
2. **Pick ONE pilot team** for the first 60 days. Justify why this team and not the obvious choice. Specify the workflow that will change, the AI surface and model, and the weekly demo cadence.
3. **Design ONE org change** to make in month 3. Could be a role, a reporting line, a review gate, or a kill of an existing role. One change, justified against what you would lose.
4. **Specify the training rollout.** Format (cadence, who teaches, what gets demo'd), the public-mistake protocol, and how you'll know in 90 days whether it's compounding or theatre.
5. **Pick the ONE behavior** you will measure as the proof of transformation. State the baseline, the 6-month target, and how you'll capture the number weekly without it becoming reportable theater.
6. **Anticipate the failure mode.** What is the single likeliest way this plan dies in months 4-5, and the one guardrail you've built for it?

At the bottom, a one-paragraph executive summary the CEO can forward to the board, and a single bullet titled **'What I would cut if budget halved'** because the CFO will ask.

No buzzwords. No 'AI-first culture'. No values posters. If you write 'transformation journey' once, the CEO is going back to the lift.
